What slows a Columbus sale

Most slowdowns come from people outside your control, such as a lender waiting on approval, an appraiser with a full calendar, or a repair list that keeps growing after the inspection. A direct cash sale avoids most of them, though a fairly priced listing can still sell briskly in Franklin County.

Whatever path you pick, pin down three facts first: the payoff on any mortgage, the year's tax status, and the school district and municipality for the parcel. The city spills across so many districts and suburban borders that buyers ask about all three right away.

City limits and school districts

No Ohio city covers more ground than Columbus, a result of annexing suburbs that needed city water lines. The city measures about 223 square miles, with 4,116 people per square mile at the 2020 census. Growth has continued: 938,396 residents in mid-2025, a 3.6% gain on the 906,215 base of April 2020 and far above the 787,033 counted in 2010.

Annexation crossed many school and township lines, so a Columbus address may fall in Columbus City Schools or in South-Western, Dublin, Hilliard, New Albany-Plain, Westerville or Worthington. Put the correct district on your listing sheet. Columbus City Schools alone runs 142 elementary, middle and high schools, and the suburban districts typically serve one or more townships, sometimes crossing municipal lines. A buyer with children will check the boundary against the district's own map, so give the street address exactly as the county records it.

Neighborhoods buyers ask about

Best known are the Arena District, Brewery District, Clintonville, Franklinton, German Village, the Short North and Victorian Village, each with its own mix of houses and buyers. Victorian Village is known for its Victorian houses facing Goodale Park.

  • Core neighborhoods: confirm the exact name buyers use for your block, since listings are searched by neighborhood.
  • Outer areas: confirm the school district and whether the parcel is inside Columbus or a neighboring suburb.
  • Riverside and creek-side parcels: the region has a history of flooding, including the Great Flood of 1913, so ask the city or county about flood-zone status before you list a low-lying house.

Home values and households

On the 2020-2024 survey, the median owner-occupied Columbus home is worth $252,900. Owners occupy 44.1% of homes across 390,528 households that average 2.28 people. Rent typically runs $1,295 a month, and the middle household earns $66,082.

As the state capital, Columbus gets most of its jobs from government, and Ohio State University with its Wexner Medical Center keeps demand steady near campus and downtown.

Franklin County deed charges

The conveyance fee is $3 per $1,000, made up of $1 for the state and $2 for the county commissioners.

Franklin County Auditor transfer tax and conveyance fee schedule

Conveyance fee when the grantor receives the homestead exemption$1 per $1,000, because the county's permissive part is waived

Transfer tax$0.50 on every non-exempt transfer
Exempt transfersOnly the $0.50 transfer tax
Accepted paymentCash, business check or cashier's check payable to the Franklin County Auditor

Personal checks are refused, and the sale amount is rounded up to the next $100. The department moves more than 30,000 transfers each year, and its number is 614-525-3253. Ohio Revised Code 319.202 and 319.54(G)(3) define which transfers are exempt.

Streets and highways

Street numbering radiates from Broad and High Streets downtown, climbing at about 700 numbers to the mile. Interstate 70 runs east and west, Interstate 71 runs north and southwest, and the two share about a mile and a half downtown at the spot locals call The Split, a known rush-hour choke point. Workers average 21.5 minutes to get to a job.

Mention how close the house is to an interstate ramp, and to the Split, because both shape the commute a buyer pictures.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Columbus houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Property tax and the homestead exemption

Property tax in Franklin County is paid in two installments, and a bill that never arrived is no excuse for paying late. Owners with no bill in hand should call 614-525-3438. At closing, the settlement statement divides the tax between buyer and seller, and your escrow officer can walk through that entry.

The standard homestead exemption is a credit aimed at older or disabled owners: age 65 by the end of the year being applied for, or total and permanent disability on January 1, plus primary residence and a qualifying income. A richer version with no income test goes to owners rated 100% disabled from military service, and it removes the tax on $50,000 of appraised value. Because a seller who holds the exemption cuts the conveyance fee to $1 per $1,000, check the Auditor's property search for the Homestead Credit status before closing.

  • Auditor's property search: lists the Homestead Credit status of your parcel.
  • Treasurer: confirms the status of the year's tax and any bill you did not receive.
  • Closing statement: shows the buyer-seller tax split before you sign.

Short-term rentals and the disclosure form

For nightly rentals, the short-term rental permit comes from the License Section of Building and Zoning Services at 4252 Groves Road, phone 614-645-8366. A house that was ever advertised on a booking platform invites buyer questions about that permit.

Revised Code 5302.30 sets the disclosure form for residences of up to four units, excusing court-ordered sales, estate fiduciaries and gifts to direct-line relatives. Severe thunderstorms and the occasional tornado can hit in spring, so known roof or hail damage belongs on the disclosure form.

From accepted offer to closing

After you accept an offer, an escrow officer opens the file, orders the title search and prepares the deed. Pull together your latest tax bill, mortgage payoff details, and permits or receipts for past work. If the property was a short-term rental or has a tenant, bring those records too.

On closing day you sign the deed in front of a notary, the buyer's money comes in, and the escrow officer clears your loan, splits the year's tax and wires you what is left. The deed then goes to the Franklin County Auditor for the conveyance fee and transfer stamp before the recorder files it. With cash there is usually no lender appraisal, so one frequent cause of delay disappears.

Rank offers by what lands in your account after the conveyance fee, the tax split and any repair credit, and write the closing date into the contract.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

How are conveyance fees figured in Franklin County?

At $3 for each $1,000 of price, with a $3 floor and a $0.50 transfer tax. A grantor who holds the homestead exemption at transfer pays $1 per $1,000 instead.

Does the Auditor take personal checks?

No. Cash, business checks and cashier's checks made out to the Franklin County Auditor are accepted, and the amount must be exact or the transfer will not process.

Could my Columbus house be in a suburban school district?

Yes, depending on the parcel. Columbus City Schools is the biggest system at 55,000 pupils, yet parts of the city belong to South-Western, Dublin, Hilliard, New Albany-Plain, Westerville or Worthington. Check your tax bill or ask the county.

My Columbus house used to be a short-term rental. Does that affect the sale?

The permit applies to operating the rental, and the License Section of Building and Zoning Services issues it. Ask that office at 614-645-8366 whether yours is current, since a buyer is likely to ask.

What if my Franklin County tax bill never arrived?

Call the treasurer at 614-525-3438. A bill that never showed up does not erase penalty and interest.

Selling a Cleveland house quickly

A cash buyer purchasing the house as it stands is the quickest path, while a conventional listing gives the most exposure but depends on showings and the buyer's loan. Cleveland owners dealing with an inheritance, a tenant problem, a code notice or a house that needs major work often ask for cash offers first and compare them with a listing price.

Compare offers on net proceeds, not headline price. Ask each buyer what repairs they expect you to make, who pays the Cuyahoga County transfer charges, and what closing date they will put in writing. A house with an open city violation, an unregistered rental or a lien changes those answers, so sort out the paperwork described below before you accept anything.

  • Which repairs, if any, the buyer expects before closing.
  • Who pays the county transfer charges and the recording fee.
  • The closing date, in writing, and what happens to your deposit if it slips.

Cleveland housing numbers

The 2025 estimate is 363,608 residents, which is 2.4% below the April 2020 base of 372,624 and well below the 396,815 counted in 2010. The 1950 census recorded 914,808 people.

  • Median value of owner-occupied homes, 2020-2024: $102,000.
  • Owners live in 41.7% of homes; the city has 169,683 households.
  • Median gross rent: $945. Median household income: $40,801.

A low median means many Cleveland sales are small-dollar deals where a few thousand dollars of repair cost or back charges matter a great deal. Ask any buyer for a written estimate of what they will deduct and why.

East Side, West Side and the city line

Clevelanders sort themselves by the Cuyahoga River into East Side and West Side, and the City Planning Commission recognizes 34 neighborhoods. West Side names include Ohio City, Detroit-Shoreway, Tremont, Edgewater, Old Brooklyn and the four sections of West Park. The East Side includes Buckeye-Shaker, Glenville, Hough, Collinwood, Lee-Miles, Mount Pleasant, St. Clair-Superior and University Circle, with Slavic Village treated on its own.

The city covers about 77.7 square miles of land on bluffs above Lake Erie, cut by the Cuyahoga River, Big Creek and Euclid Creek, and it shares borders with Lakewood, Shaker Heights, Cleveland Heights, South Euclid, Parma and many other suburbs. Because so many municipalities touch the city line, confirm on your tax bill that the address is billed as Cleveland.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Cleveland house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Lake weather and older houses

Lake Erie moderates temperatures but drives heavy snow on the East Side. Lake-effect snow typically arrives from mid-November until the lake surface freezes, usually in late January or early February. The far West Side has reached 100 inches of seasonal snowfall only three times since records began in 1893, while the hills on the east side regularly approach that total.

Buyers inspecting an older East Side house will look closely at the roof, flashing, gutters and basement walls. If you replaced any of these, keep the invoice. If you did not, expect the price discussion to include them.

Rental registration before you sell

A seller who rents the house out must have it registered with the city every year, and skipping the occupancy certificate may lead to civil or criminal enforcement. All owners of non-owner-occupied residential property register, at $70 per unit, including units used by relatives or friends rent-free. Applications go through the city's Citizens Access Portal.

Once the documents are in, the city issues a Certificate Approving Rental Occupancy. The property cannot have open code violations, taxes must be paid or on a county payment plan, and any outstanding city fees must be cleared. Renewal applications open after January 1 with fees due by March 31. An empty unit uses Vacant Property Registration instead. Records Administration answers questions at 216-664-2825.

Highways and schools

Interstates 71, 77, 90, 480 and 490 serve the city, and Cleveland Hopkins International Airport is on the West Side. Workers spend 22.5 minutes getting to work on average. The public school system is the Cleveland Metropolitan School District, although about one square mile of the Buckeye-Shaker area belongs to the Shaker Heights City School District.

Taxes, recording and disclosure

The Cuyahoga County Fiscal Office records deeds and also issues the statement-of-value forms, DTE 100 or the exemption version DTE 100-EX, which must travel with every transfer. Its Transfer and Recording division is at 2079 E. Ninth Street and can be reached at 216-443-2060. The county raised its standard recording fee in October 2024 under Senate Bill 94, so ask your closing agent for the figure on your deed's page count.

Tax bills come from the county treasurer, and House Bill 920 cuts effective rates as values rise after reappraisals. For a Cleveland rental, registration asks for proof that taxes are paid or on a payment plan in good standing, and the treasurer's taxpayer services line, 216-443-7400, handles payment plans.

The state disclosure statute, Revised Code 5302.30, covers most sales of homes with up to four units and exempts estate and court-ordered transfers, so owners selling an inherited house should ask an attorney whether it applies.

On closing day you sign the deed before a notary, the title company pays off liens and unpaid taxes from your proceeds, and the county records the deed afterward. Bring identification and your keys.

What a cash sale skips

A cash purchase skips the lender's appraisal, the buyer's financing contingency and, in most cases, the repair list that follows an inspection. For a Cleveland house with deferred maintenance, that can mean the difference between closing in a short window and waiting through several rounds of renegotiation.

It does not skip the paperwork. Whoever buys, the deed still needs a statement of value, the county still records it, and any lien, unpaid tax or open code violation has to be dealt with at or before closing. Ask for a payoff figure early, gather your tax bill and mortgage statement, and have the title company list every deduction before you sign. If the house is a registered rental, bring the registration and the occupancy certificate so the buyer can see the property is in good standing.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need to register my Cleveland rental before I sell it?

Yes, if it is rented, the city expects annual registration at $70 per unit, and it will not issue a Certificate Approving Rental Occupancy while code violations are open. A vacant unit is registered as a vacant property instead.

When are Cleveland rental registration fees due?

Renewal applications can be filed any time after January 1, and all fees must be paid by March 31. New rentals register before tenants move in, at any point in the year.

Does my Cleveland street fall in a different school district?

Nearly all of the city is in the Cleveland Metropolitan School District. About one square mile of the Buckeye-Shaker neighborhood is in the Shaker Heights City School District, so check the street if you live there.

What does a Lead Safe Certificate have to do with selling?

The city requires a Lead Safe Certificate, valid for 2 years or 20 years, for rental units built before 1978, and it must be uploaded with the rental registration. A buyer who plans to keep the unit rented will ask whether you hold one.

Which county office records my Cleveland deed?

The Fiscal Office's Transfer and Recording division, 2079 E. Ninth Street, 4th floor, takes it with a DTE 100 or DTE 100-EX form attached. Closing agents normally carry it over for you.

Selling in Cincinnati?

Ways to sell fast in Cincinnati

Cincinnati owners generally pick between a brokerage listing, a for-sale-by-owner sale and a direct purchase by a cash buyer. Each trades days on market, repair spending and fees in its own way, and owners who want a fixed closing date or who hold a worn-out house tend to weigh all three.

A brokerage listing reaches the most shoppers, though it also brings open houses, inspection repair requests and an appraisal ordered by the buyer's lender. A cash purchase drops most of those steps because the buyer takes the property in whatever shape it is in. Every route ends at the same Hamilton County deed and transfer paperwork, described further down.

  • Brokerage listing: the broadest audience, a commission owed at closing, and a schedule tied to the buyer's loan.
  • For sale by owner: the commission stays with you, while the contract, disclosure form and title coordination land on your desk.
  • Cash purchase: little or no repair haggling and fewer visits, with the number driven by the buyer's read of the property's current state.

Hills, neighborhoods and pricing

The city rests above the Ohio River's northern shore and spreads across hills, bluffs and low ridges, so lot slope and street access vary a lot from one address to the next. Fifty-two neighborhoods make up the city, many of them former villages that were annexed and kept their names, such as Walnut Hills and Mount Auburn. Westwood has the largest population, and CUF and Price Hill are also large. Over-the-Rhine, near downtown, holds one of the largest intact historic districts in the country, with ornate brick buildings put up by German immigrants between 1865 and the 1880s.

Look at your parcel record before you list. Norwood, Elmwood Place and St. Bernard are separate municipalities that sit entirely inside Cincinnati's boundaries, so confirm which municipality your parcel is in. Your deed or the county auditor's parcel record shows the taxing district.

Cincinnati homes by the numbers

Renters outnumber owners here. With owners living in fewer than four of every ten homes, many Cincinnati deals involve landlords as well as families.

Commutes and highways

Mean travel time to work is 22.4 minutes. Interstates 71, 74 and 75 pass through the area, Interstate 275 circles it as an 85-mile beltway, and Interstate 471 runs a spur into Kentucky. Buyers often ask how far the nearest ramp is, so have that answer ready.

Schools come up in almost every showing. Cincinnati Public Schools runs 18 high schools with citywide acceptance, including Walnut Hills High School and the School for Creative and Performing Arts.

City rules for a house you sell or rent out

Three programs matter most to sellers: vacant building registration, short-term rental registration and the state's disclosure form. None of them replace a check with the city's Buildings and Inspections office if the house has open violations.

  • Vacant building registration: a building that sits vacant for 180 days or more must be secured, insured and registered. Registration is due within thirty days of the property qualifying or of a new owner taking title, whichever is later, and the certificate lasts six months. Residential buildings with no more than four units need general liability coverage of at least $300,000. Owners register through ezTrak.
  • Short-term rentals: a house offered on a hosting platform for stays under thirty consecutive days must be registered before it operates. The registration lasts three years, and the registration ID has to appear in every listing. Where a platform has no collection agreement, the operator reports excise tax at 7% of gross revenues. The Treasury license desk is at 801 Plum Street, Room 202, phone 513-352-3224.
  • State disclosure form: Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 requires a signed condition report for sales of homes with up to four dwelling units. Exemptions cover, among others, estate fiduciaries and heirs who never lived there.

An empty house after an inheritance or a move calls for a look at the vacancy rules first, since a missed filing can bring fines.

Hamilton County deed charges

Deed transfer in Hamilton County carries a conveyance and permissive fee of $3.00 per thousand dollars of the price, plus a $.50 transfer fee for each parcel on the deed.

Payment goes in as cash or a check payable to the Hamilton County Auditor, and a check has to equal the amount owed because the office cannot return change on one. Recording charges belong to another office and stay out of that check. Each deed also needs the statement of value on DTE form 100, or an exemption statement, filed by the grantee or a representative. Escrow agents usually carry this paperwork over, so find out who at yours will.

Property tax is a separate bill from the treasurer, paid in two halves, one due in winter and one in summer. The settlement statement shows how the year's tax is divided, so read that line closely, and call the Hamilton County Treasurer at 513-946-4800 if a bill is missing.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Cincinnati houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Weather and inspections

Rain falls in every month here, with monthly precipitation between roughly three and five inches. Freeze-thaw cycles in winter and heavy summer storms are hard on roofs, gutters and masonry, and hillside lots send water toward foundations.

Walk the exterior before listing, check the basement for staining, and keep a list of repairs already made. A past fix written on the form reads better than one an inspector uncovers. If you have a stack of repairs you would rather not manage, a cash buyer will price them in, and you can close on a date you pick instead of one tied to a lender's appraisal.

From offer to closing

After you accept an offer, an escrow officer opens the file, orders the title search and prepares the deed. Gather your tax bills, any city notices and receipts for repairs. If the house is empty or rented, bring the registration records as well. You sign the deed, the buyer funds the purchase, and the escrow agent pays off your loan and sends the balance to you.

Frequently asked questions

Must a Cincinnati seller fix the house first?

Ohio's disclosure law asks you to describe known defects, and it does not itself order repairs. Open code violations are different, so ask Buildings and Inspections about any notice in hand. Cash buyers purchase houses with their problems, which is why owners of damaged homes look at them.

Does an heir have to complete the Ohio disclosure form?

Often not. Section 5302.30 exempts estate fiduciaries, and also a transferor who has not lived in the house during the past year and acquired it by inheritance or devise. Check with a probate attorney before skipping it.

What are Hamilton County's deed transfer charges?

$3.00 per thousand dollars of the price and $.50 per parcel. Recording is paid elsewhere, so request the full closing figure from your escrow officer.

Is a vacant Cincinnati house harder to sell?

It can be sold, but the registration clock matters. Once a building has stood vacant 180 days, it must be registered with Buildings and Inspections, and a buyer who takes title has thirty days to file. Filing runs through ezTrak, and CincyVBR@cincinnati-oh.gov takes questions.

Where do I register a Cincinnati short-term rental?

Use the Treasury license desk at 801 Plum Street, Room 202, phone 513-352-3224, email Treasury.License@cincinnati-oh.gov. A registration runs three years, and its ID goes in every listing.

Vacant houses, land contracts and short-term rentals

Three city rules can touch a sale.

  • Vacant buildings: Municipal Code 1767 requires owners to register a vacant residential building within 30 days and renew each year. A 2025 update cut the annual fee from $200 to $100. Owners who skip registration face daily fines, notices of liability and court action.
  • Land installment contracts: Municipal Code 1765 demands a Certificate of Property Code Compliance when a home of one to three units is sold on a land installment contract. The city charges $120 to apply, and a report from a city-registered home inspector is due within 30 days. If you'd rather have the city inspect, the fee is $300.
  • Short-term rentals: each unit needs a $50 annual permit and proof of $1,000,000 in general liability coverage. Running or advertising a listing without one draws $100 per week, capped at $500.

Selling an unregistered vacant house? Ask the Division of Code Compliance about open fines first. A title search can turn them up.

Selling a Toledo rental

Lead Safe Toledo applies to rentals of one to four units built before 1978. Owners register with the Lucas County Auditor's rental registry, hire a registered lead inspector for clearance, correct hazards and apply for the certificate. A lead inspection costs about $400 in Toledo, and the certificate must exist before a new tenant moves in.

A buyer who takes over an uncertified rental has to finish that work before a new tenant arrives. A recorded land contract generally isn't treated as a rental, but a lease with an option to purchase is. Gather the certificate, the registry confirmation and the leases before you negotiate.

Deed transfer through Lucas County

A transfer moves through three desks inside One Government Center. The Engineer's Tax Map Department approves the legal description and the Recorder checks fee amounts, both on the 7th floor. Then the deed, conveyance form and recorder fees go to the Auditor on the 6th. Buyer and seller should attend with unexpired government photo ID. The Auditor answers questions at 419-213-4406.

  • Conveyance Fee: $4.00 per $1,000 of the sale price.
  • Transfer Fee: $0.50 per parcel.
  • Recording: $39.00 for the first two deed pages, $8.00 for each page beyond that, and possible postage.

Under Ohio Revised Code 322.02 the county transfer tax falls on the grantor. The Auditor's staff can't draft a deed, so hire an attorney. A mistake can mean a rejected filing now or a title problem later.

Does the Ohio disclosure rule cover a land contract?

Yes. The statute reaches sales, land installment contracts, exchanges and lease-purchase deals on homes with up to four units, and it treats the transfer as happening when the first contract is signed. Put the completed form in the buyer's hands before that signature.

Preparing a Toledo house for a fast sale

Before you call any buyer, sort out which rule above applies to your house. A vacant house needs its registration current. A rental needs its lead certificate, registry confirmation and leases. A land contract sale needs the compliance certificate. Knowing this up front keeps you from agreeing to a date the city's process can't meet.

On the county side, plan a visit to One Government Center with ID and a draft deed from your attorney. Ask the Auditor's office what they need before you go, because the Tax Map Department and the Recorder both have to sign off before the Auditor accepts the paperwork.

A cash purchase skips the repair list and the wait for a buyer's financing, but it doesn't skip any of the city or county steps. Those apply to every sale, whether the buyer pays cash or uses a loan, so build them into your timeline from the start.

A rough order of work helps. Start with the city items, since registrations and certificates take the longest. Next, line up an attorney for the deed and ask for the conveyance form at the same time. Then confirm with the Auditor which fees apply at your price, and pick up the unexpired photo ID you'll both need to bring. Finally, compare offers on net proceeds after the transfer tax, recording charges and any city fines, not just on the headline number.

If tenants live in the house, tell any buyer early. Leases, the registry confirmation and the lead certificate all affect what an investor will pay, and a buyer who finds those documents missing late in the process usually asks for a lower price or walks away. Collecting everything in one folder before the first call saves days.

Frequently asked questions

How much is the Lucas County conveyance fee?

The fee is $4.00 per $1,000 of the sale price, plus $0.50 per parcel. Under state law the grantor (the seller) bears the transfer tax.

Do I have to register a vacant house in Toledo?

Yes, when it is a vacant residential building. Code 1767 sets a 30-day window, annual renewal and a $100 fee, and registering does not wipe out existing code violations.

Does Toledo require an inspection when I sell?

Only some sales do. A land installment contract sale needs a Certificate of Property Code Compliance. For an ordinary sale, ask the Division of Building Inspection what applies to your property type, and expect the buyer to order a private inspection.

Can I sell a Toledo rental that lacks a lead certificate?

Yes, but the certificate has to exist before a new tenant moves in. A buyer who plans to rent will weigh the clearance inspection, which costs about $400.

Where do I record a Toledo deed?

At One Government Center, in this order: Tax Map Department, Recorder, Auditor. Recording is $39.00 for two pages, with $8.00 for each page added.

Ways Akron owners sell a house quickly

Most sellers weigh three options: an agent's listing, a sale handled on your own, or a cash offer from an investor. The options differ in speed, net proceeds and workload, and the house's condition often settles the question.

  • An agent listing suits a house that shows well. Expect photos, open showings, an inspection and a lender's appraisal before the buyer closes.
  • Selling it yourself skips the agent's commission, but you set the price, screen buyers and manage the contract.
  • A cash purchase can close whenever both sides agree, and the buyer may take the house as it stands, a trade-off that shows in the price.

Whichever route you choose, the deed ends up at the Summit County Fiscal Office. Ask for any offer in writing first, with the price, the closing date and who pays which closing costs.

Akron housing market in brief

Akron is the seat of Summit County, about 40 miles south of Cleveland. The 2025 estimate is 189,691 residents. Owners live in 50.7 percent of Akron's homes, so about half of all households rent, and a market shaped by that split means many buyers are investors and landlords.

Winter wear on an Akron house

Akron gets about 47.2 inches of snow in a typical season, and roughly 40 days a year never climb above freezing. Snow, thaw cycles and damp air are hard on roofs, gutters, foundation walls and basements. Look at those first, and decide whether to repair before listing or to price the house as is. A buyer's inspector will check the same spots.

Landlord rules and code violations

Landlords must register rentals with the city each year. A rental is any dwelling or rooming unit that the titleholder does not occupy. The deadline is January 31, after which a $25 per unit late fee applies. The city's registration table lists 39,363 units and 4,000 owners for 2023.

If you inherited a rental or want to sell with tenants in place, confirm the registration first. The Housing Compliance Division enforces the Environmental Health Housing Code. Anyone can report a possible violation through 3-1-1; an inspector then investigates, and an order to repair gives a deadline for fixes. Ignoring an order invites legal proceedings and fines, so clear open orders or tell a buyer about them.

How a deed gets recorded after an Akron sale

The Summit County Fiscal Office, Recording Division, takes deeds at 175 South Main Street, 4th Floor, Akron 44308, phone 330-643-2712. Turnaround is three to five working days. Anyone can search recorded documents online back to 1988, and an archive viewer covers 1840 to 1988. Title searches are not part of the office's work.

  • Filing the instrument: $34.00 covers the first two pages, and each page beyond that is $8.00 (ORC 317.32).
  • The conveyance fee equals $4.00 for every $1000 of price, where the price is first rounded up to a multiple of $100.
  • A lot fee of 50 cents applies to each lot named in the legal description, exempt transfer or not.
  • A document that fails the office's standards draws a $20.00 non-compliant fee under ORC 317.114.

A new deed's route runs through the Tax Map Department first for the legal description, then the Conveyance Department, then Recording. Ask your closing attorney or title company who will walk it through.

Property tax payments and late costs

The Fiscal Office's Treasurers Division, on the third floor of the Ohio Building at 175 S. Main St., takes walk-in payments from 7:30 am to 4:00 pm on weekdays. Other routes exist: a mailed check, a participating bank while a collection is open, or a phone or web payment on which a vendor adds a service charge.

No grace period exists, and a missing bill is no excuse. An unpaid first half draws a 10 percent penalty, and after the second-half date a further 10 percent lands on all unpaid current taxes. Tax certificate lien sales occur each year in late October. Your title company will request a payoff before closing.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Akron houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Repair first or sell as is?

This one turns on how much time and spare cash you have. A roof that leaks or a basement that stays damp can scare off anyone who needs a mortgage, because the appraiser and the inspector write down what they see. Fixing it widens your buyer pool, but the work takes weeks, you pay up front, and the sale price may not repay you.

Leaving the house untouched gives up some price in exchange for a sure date. Investors paying cash build the repair bill into their number, so you skip contractor bids and any second haggle after an inspection. Collect two offers and compare what you would pocket after commissions, repairs and the extra months of mortgage, tax and utility bills.

What a cash buyer does not skip

Cash removes the loan approval, the appraisal and usually the open houses. The legal work stays. You still sign the deed in front of a notary, the Summit County Fiscal Office still collects its conveyance fee and records the transfer, and the title company still pays off unpaid property tax from your proceeds. A repair order from the city does not vanish either, so clear it or put it in writing for the buyer.

If tenants live in the house

A tenant-occupied sale can work well when the buyer is another landlord. That buyer will care about a current registration with the city, a clean code history and a paid tax bill. Pull together the lease, your registration confirmation and any repair orders before you take calls, and give tenants notice before anyone tours the unit.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

What happens between offer and closing

After you say yes to an offer, a title company starts a file. It requests the tax payoff, reviews what is recorded against the parcel, and asks about code orders and rental registration. Your signed deed then goes to the Fiscal Office. Closing day is whatever date you and a cash buyer pick, while a buyer with a loan waits on the lender.

Before signing a contract, learn whether the house carries an open repair order, a tax balance or an unregistered rental unit. Each costs less to sort out early.

Frequently asked questions

How soon can an Akron sale close?

That depends on the route you choose. An agent-led listing moves through showings, inspections and a lender's review, while a cash sale can close on an agreed date. After closing, recording takes three to five working days at the Summit County Fiscal Office.

Must I register a rental house with Akron before selling?

Akron requires rental units to be registered every year by January 31, with a $25 per unit late fee afterward. Confirm yours is current before you list a house with tenants.

Where is a deed for an Akron home recorded?

At the Summit County Fiscal Office, Recording Division, 175 South Main Street, 4th Floor, phone 330-643-2712. Recorded documents can be searched online back to 1988.

What is the penalty for paying Akron property tax late?

An unpaid first half draws 10 percent, and a further 10 percent follows on unpaid current taxes after the second-half date. There is no grace period.

How do I find out about open housing code orders on an Akron property?

Call the Housing Compliance Division at 330-375-2366 or dial 3-1-1. A repair order carries a compliance date, and ignoring one can lead to legal proceedings and fines.

Selling a house in Dayton

A Dayton seller can list with an agent, sell without one, or accept a cash purchase. Whichever route you pick, the sale runs through a city disclosure step that most Ohio cities don't have. Dayton is the Montgomery County seat, and the population is 136,688 for July 2025, down slightly from 137,644 in 2020. It is the sixth-most populous city in Ohio.

Housing here is inexpensive and mostly rented. The median value of an owner-occupied home is $100,600, and 48.4 percent of households own, so just over half rent. Median gross rent is $918, and median monthly owner cost with a mortgage is $1,147. With that many renters, plenty of Dayton houses are sold by landlords with tenants still inside, and many others come out of estates. Both situations are covered below.

Population peaked at 262,332 in 1960, so many blocks were built for a city far larger than today's. Buyers know it, and they look hard at roof age, windows and past repairs, especially in the older historic neighborhoods such as Oregon District, Dayton View, Grafton Hill and South Park. If you own in one of those areas, collect repair invoices before you list.

The City of Dayton Certificate of Disclosure

Any sale of a property inside the city requires a Certificate of Disclosure that tells the buyer about open housing code violations. Look at the parcel number: if it starts with R72 or R726, the property is in Dayton and the form must be filed. The form exists to inform the buyer. It isn't meant to stop a sale.

  • With no open violations, the seller signs and supplies the buyer's contact details.
  • With open violations, the form must show the violation or structural nuisance status, a flat $60 fee is paid (not per violation), and both parties sign, with the buyer's signature notarized.
  • The buyer agrees either that the violations are corrected before the sale or that the buyer will make the listed repairs within 90 days.
  • The title company usually asks the city for violation information and pending bills 7 to 10 business days before closing.

Selling doesn't remove violations. They transfer with the house, which is why the buyer has to sign on to the repairs. The city's FAQ lists exceptions for three types of transfer, so ask the city whether yours is one of them.

Code violations and nuisance properties

The Division of Housing and Inspections enforces the housing ordinance and the public nuisance ordinance. Its work also covers trees and trash, non-residential exterior maintenance, and abandoned or junk vehicles. For an open violation notice or citation, call 937-333-3867 or 937-333-8645.

Two online tools let you see what a buyer can see. The Dayton Housing Tracker searches by address or neighborhood, and the Dayton Housing Condition Survey portal shows housing conditions by neighborhood. Complaints and service requests go through Dayton Delivers.

Look up your own address before you list. If a citation is on file, you can fix it, price around it, or plan the disclosure form with the buyer. Finding it early is far cheaper than finding it when the title company calls the city a week or two before closing.

Storm history and the Ohio condition form

Dayton has hot, humid summers and cold winters, and severe thunderstorms, floods, blizzards and tornadoes are all possible. On Memorial Day 2019, a tornado outbreak put 15 tornadoes on the ground in the Dayton area, including an EF4 that tore through Brookville, Trotwood, Dayton, Northridge and Riverside.

Roofs, siding and basements are where buyers look for storm history. Keep repair invoices, insurance claim paperwork and contractor names in one folder. That lets you answer the state disclosure form with documents instead of memory, and it shortens the back and forth after an inspection.

Selling a rental in Dayton

A landlord selling a rental should check city permit rules, tenant protections and short-term use before setting a price. Dayton requires a contractor registered with the city for plumbing, electrical and HVAC work on rental property, on an unoccupied house that will be rented, and on duplexes, even where the owner lives in one half. Owner-occupants may do some of that work themselves after getting the right permits.

The city's FAQ also describes source of income rules: landlords can't refuse a prospective tenant because rent comes from vouchers, subsidies, benefits or other public assistance. A sale doesn't end a lease, so read it for the end date and notice terms and tell buyers early.

Short-term rentals are stays under 30 consecutive days. The city has no registration system for them and handles concerns case by case. If your buyer plans to use the house that way, ask the city planning office what applies before you sign.

Montgomery County deed transfer costs

The Montgomery County Auditor handles the deed transfer, and the Recorder records the deed afterward.

Montgomery County deed transfer and recording rates

The deed goes to the Auditor's Deed Transfer Department for a transfer stamp before it reaches the Recorder. Questions go to the deed transfer line at 937-225-4373. Electronic filing is available through two named e-recording services, and most sellers let the title company handle it.

What Ohio law adds to the city form

State law (R.C. 5302.30) has the seller of a one-to-four-unit home fill out Ohio's own condition form and deliver a signed copy. If the buyer sees it only after a contract is signed, a written cancellation is allowed for three business days after receipt, ending no later than thirty days from acceptance or closing, whichever is first.

The state form doesn't replace Dayton's certificate. You need both. The city's certificate concerns open code violations, while the state form covers physical condition items such as the roof, basement and plumbing. Hand over the state form early, at the listing stage, so a late delivery can't give the buyer a way out of the contract.

A step by step plan for a Dayton sale

Start by checking the parcel number so you know the city certificate applies. Look up your address on the Dayton Housing Tracker, then call Housing and Inspections about anything open. Next, gather the paperwork a buyer or title company will ask for: repair invoices, insurance claims, any lease, and the state condition form.

Once you have a contract, the title company requests violation information and pending bills from the city, usually 7 to 10 business days before closing. Expect the deed to go through the Auditor for the transfer stamp and then to the Recorder. Costs at the county level are the conveyance fee, the per-parcel charge and the recording fee in the table above.

A cash buyer skips the lender's appraisal and repair demands, so the timeline is often shorter. That helps with an estate, a tenant-occupied house or a property with open violations. The city certificate and the state form still apply, so ask every buyer to put the price, the closing date and who pays each cost in writing, then compare offers side by side.

Frequently asked questions

How do I know if my Dayton property needs the city disclosure?

Check the parcel number. A number beginning with R72 or R726 is inside the City of Dayton and requires a Certificate of Disclosure. The city's FAQ lists exceptions for three types of transfer.

What does an open violation cost me at sale?

The city charges a flat $60 fee with the disclosure form when there is an open violation, not a per-violation fee. The buyer must also sign before a notary and agree to corrections within 90 days or earlier repairs.

Does selling a Dayton house clear its code violations?

No. A sale doesn't remove violations from a property. They pass to the buyer, who agrees to resolve them.

What is the Montgomery County conveyance fee?

The county charges a mandatory conveyance fee of $3 per $1,000 of the actual sale price, plus $.50 for each parcel transferred.

Does Dayton regulate Airbnb-style rentals?

The city has no system to register or regulate short-term rentals and handles concerns case by case. A short-term rental is a stay of less than 30 consecutive days.

Faster ways to sell in Parma

Parma owners can hire a broker, sell on their own, or deal with a cash buyer who takes the place flaws and all. The city is large and densely built, and it grew fastest after the war, so buyers often negotiate over items that come with age. A cash sale takes repair requests and mortgage appraisals out of the schedule.

  • Cash fits an estate house, a vacant property, missed loan payments, or repair bills you want to avoid.

Parma also keeps city registrations for rentals, vacant homes and foreclosure filings, covered below. Any of them can affect how fast a sale moves.

Parma housing figures

Parma, roughly 8 miles south of downtown Cleveland, is the biggest suburb in Ohio. The 2020 census counted 81,146 residents and the mid-2025 estimate is 78,581. The population peaked at 100,216 in 1970 and has eased down since. The city spans 20.07 square miles with about 4,000 residents per square mile, so lots are close together and the houses are mostly older. The middle-priced owned home is valued at $170,100, and roughly 72 percent of homes are occupied by their owners.

Building permits and penalties

The Building Department requires a permit before work starts, and charges an administrative penalty when work begins without one: $100 for a first offense, $300 for a second and $500 for a third. Contractors have to be registered with the department as well, with a $250 charge if they start before registration is final. Windows, siding and roofing jobs each have their own permit application, and so do fences, sheds, garages, driveways and pools.

If you replaced a roof or added a deck without a permit, settle it before you list. The city's fence application also asks for either a state-registered surveyor's boundary survey or consent from neighbors.

City registrations that can slow a sale

Parma attaches these registrations to particular property situations:

  • Residential rental registration: $150 per property, certificates lapse each December 31, and a $50 late fee applies.
  • Notification of foreclosure filing: $100 for a one-, two- or three-family residence.
  • Vacant residential property registration: $200, valid for one year.
  • Multiple dwelling registration: $100 for mixed-use buildings and apartment buildings with one to four suites.

Each of these can be completed online. Call the Building Department to learn whether any of them is attached to your address, and clear it before the buyer's title company asks.

Taxes and valuation appeals

Parma belongs to Cuyahoga County, whose Fiscal Officer sets values and whose Treasurer collects the money. Billing trails the tax year, so bills paid in 2023 belonged to tax year 2022. Each bill is due in two halves, and a late payment draws a 10 percent penalty. Ask the Treasurer for the due dates that apply this year.

Someone who paid late can ask for the penalty to be waived on DTE Form 23A. The Treasury looks first, the Fiscal Office second, and the Board of Revision rules whenever the reasonable-cause box is ticked. That ruling stands unless it is taken to the Board of Tax Appeals within 30 days.

Believe the assessed value is inflated? A valuation complaint can be filed from the start of January through March 31, and the board prefers e-filing. You must state an exact figure as your opinion of value, and the board cautions that it may raise the value when evidence supports a higher number. A denied homestead or owner-occupancy request can be appealed sixty days from the date on the denial letter. If the county has begun an expedited tax foreclosure, the house could end up at sheriff sale or with a land bank.

Recording the deed

Deeds are recorded in the Fiscal Officer's Transfer and Recording division, which wants a DTE 100 form attached to every transfer. A recording fee change took effect October 24, 2024: $39 buys two pages, and each additional page adds $8. State law also requires the seller's disclosure form under section 5302.30 unless the transfer is exempt.

The closing agent or lawyer usually files all of this. What you can do beforehand is clear any open permit, rental registration or vacant-property registration, so nothing surfaces in the title search.

Getting a Parma house ready for a quick closing

Start with a call to the Building Department. Ask whether permits are open for the roof, windows, siding, fence, shed, garage, driveway or pool, and whether a rental, vacant-property or foreclosure registration is on file for the address. A first offense for work without a permit costs $100, so it is cheaper to fix the record now than after a buyer finds it.

Next, line up the money side. Learn what you owe on the mortgage, ask the Treasurer whether any tax bill is unpaid, and decide whether a valuation complaint is worth the risk that the board raises the value. Then ask your closing agent or lawyer to draft the deed and the DTE 100 so recording is not the slow step.

Last, fill out the Ohio disclosure form honestly. Older houses in a dense suburb tend to have known quirks in the basement, the roof or the wiring, and a buyer who hears about them from you rather than from an inspector is less likely to walk away or ask for a bigger discount.

Selling a Parma house with a cash buyer

The buyer accepts the property in its present state, so you skip contractors and wait times for lender approval. The city asks for a notification of foreclosure filing at $100 for one-, two- and three-family homes. Contact the Building Department about the filing, and ask a closing agent how a sale would pay off the loan.

Can I dispute my Parma valuation before selling?

Yes. The county Board of Revision takes complaints from January through March 31, wants an exact opinion of value, and looks for proof such as a recent sale, an appraisal or contractor estimates.

The fastest sale route in Canton

A cash buyer is the quickest way out of a Canton house, and a listing with financed buyers is the slowest. Which one suits you depends on the condition of the house and your deadline.

  • Listing: the broadest exposure, best when the house photographs well. Loan-backed buyers bring appraisals and inspection requests.
  • As-is cash sale: skips showings and the buyer's repair list. The bid already subtracts the work the buyer will do.
  • Private sale: workable if you know the buyer, such as a tenant. Write the price and terms into a contract.

About half of Canton's homes are non-owner-occupied. If yours sits empty or has a tenant, the registration rules below follow the property before and after the sale.

Canton housing market

Canton is a modest-priced market, and owners occupy fewer than half of its homes. The midpoint value of an owned house is $97,800, against household income of $43,188. The 2020 census counted 70,872 residents, and the mid-2025 estimate is 69,001. The city sits about 60 miles south of Cleveland and 20 miles south of Akron.

When values are this low, a repair bill can swallow a large part of a sale price, which is one reason some owners look at direct sales.

Streets, neighborhoods and old housing

Canton's plat was recorded on November 15, 1805, and the city became the seat of Stark County in 1809. Addresses follow a grid. Tuscarawas Street splits north from south and Market Avenue splits east from west, and the quadrant letters trail the street name, as in 55th Street NE.

Named neighborhoods include Downtown, Ridgewood, Edgefield, Harter Heights, Hills and Dales, Lathrop, Shorb, and West Park. The Ridgewood Historic District became a National Register district on December 19, 1982, and its blocks have architectural interest. Nimishillen Creek and its three branches run through the city, so a creek-side lot is worth a flood-risk question to your insurer before you list.

Registering a vacant or rental house

Section 1351.03 of the city's codified ordinances requires owners of non-owner-occupied and vacant residential property to register every year with the Chief Building Official, beginning January 1. The house or unit where the owner lives is left out.

The 2025 form listed $110 per unit, for small buildings and larger ones alike. A property not registered by March 1, or within 30 days of a change in ownership, draws a fine of twice the fee per unit on top of the fee. The fee schedule can change, so request the current form from the Building Department.

  • A registered vacant house needs a clean interior and garage, mowed grass in summer, and sidewalks cleared in winter.
  • Junk vehicles, tires, and hazardous materials may not sit on the premises.
  • A new non-owner-occupied property needs an inspection.

Code Enforcement works from 424 Market Avenue North, third floor. Call 330-430-7800.

Code enforcement and your sale

Code officers investigate housing complaints on owner-occupied and rental buildings, and the division leads demolition work on abandoned and structurally unsafe buildings. Ask whether a complaint or violation is on file for your address before you list.

New software went live on October 1, 2025. Through the online portal you can search permits, schedule inspections, submit applications, and pay invoices, including non-owner-occupied registrations. Only plans and permits created from that date forward can be searched there. For older records, call 330-430-7800. The office keeps weekday hours of 8 to 11:45 in the morning and 1 to 4 in the afternoon.

If the house faces a demolition order, a condemnation, or unpaid registration fines, settle those items through the title company so the closing statement shows them.

Stark County tax relief and paperwork

Canton lies in Stark County. The county auditor values the house and runs the homestead program, while the transfer fee falls on the seller under Revised Code 319.202.

The homestead exemption shields $29,000 of market value for owners aged 65 and up, or totally and permanently disabled, with prior-year household income at or under $41,000. Disabled owners who served in the military can qualify for an enhanced amount of $58,000. Real property applications are due December 31. If the auditor denies one, form DTE 106B starts an appeal to the Board of Revision.

  • An owner who moves to another Ohio property files a fresh application, and the credit starts the next year.
  • Revised Code 5715.19 sets the March 31 window for value complaints.
  • Ask the Stark County Treasurer for the tax figure through closing.

Selling an inherited house

The state condition form in Revised Code 5302.30 applies to buildings of up to four dwellings. It carves out sales by estate fiduciaries and sales by an heir who did not live in the house for the previous year, which matters in a city where many houses pass through families. Even where the form is excused, tell the buyer what you know about leaks, repairs, and utilities, and keep notes.

Roads and winter wear on houses

Interstate 77 passes through town, and U.S. Routes 30 and 62 lead to Wooster, East Liverpool, Millersburg, and Youngstown. Most students attend Canton City Schools, though part of northern Canton falls in Plain Local and another area overlaps Canton Local. Winters bring about 47.7 inches of snow per season, so buyers look closely at roofs, gutters, and furnaces.

From accepted offer to closing day

Once you accept an offer, a title company or closing agent opens the file. They search the title, confirm who owns the parcel, and prepare the deed and the settlement statement. Ask for a draft of that statement before closing day so each line, including the seller-paid transfer fee, is familiar.

Bring photo identification, all keys, and any paperwork on repairs. If the house is vacant or rented, bring the registration form and the inspection record as well, since a buyer will want proof the property is in good standing. You sign the deed before a notary, and the title company pays off any mortgage, unpaid taxes, and fines from your proceeds.

  • Walk the house for code issues before you list, so an open complaint does not surprise you.
  • Gather the Stark County tax bill and any homestead paperwork for the title company.
  • Take photos of the house on the day you hand over keys.

With a cash buyer, you can often skip staging, showings, and the lender's appraisal, and you can pick a closing date that fits your move. Compare bids by what you net, not by the headline number, and have the contract spell out who pays each cost.

Do I register my Canton rental before I sell it?

Yes, when the house is non-owner-occupied or vacant. Section 1351.03 calls for yearly registration, with a March 1 late date on the 2025 form. Code Enforcement at 330-430-7800 can confirm where your property stands.

What happens to the registration fee if I sell in the middle of the year?

The 2025 form asks for registration within 30 days of obtaining ownership, so the buyer has that window. Ask the Building Department how a mid-year sale affects your year's fee.

Can a vacant house in Canton sell as-is?

Yes. Cash buyers purchase vacant houses regularly. Until the deed passes, a registered vacant property must stay clean, mowed, and clear of snow and junk. Complete the Ohio disclosure form unless your transfer is excluded.

Whose cost is the transfer fee on a Canton sale?

The seller. It is a seller cost under Revised Code 319.202 and appears on the settlement statement.

Where do Stark County owners appeal a value or a homestead denial?

Both appeals travel through the auditor to the Board of Revision. Value complaints follow the March 31 rule in Revised Code 5715.19, and homestead denials use form DTE 106B.

Selling a Lorain house without a long wait

Lorain sellers usually weigh three routes: list with an agent, sell to someone they already know, or sell to a company that pays cash and asks for no repairs. Houses here run from lakefront blocks near Lakeview Park to older streets that grew up around the steel mill, so the condition of the house and the street both affect how fast a sale moves.

An open-market listing reaches the most buyers, but a financed buyer usually brings an appraisal and a repair list with them. A cash sale skips both, and you can leave the painting and fixing undone. Weigh any difference in price against what the house costs you every month in taxes, insurance and utilities while it sits.

Three situations come with their own city or county steps, covered further down:

  • Vacant houses need to be registered with the city.
  • A house with an active foreclosure case needs a city bond.
  • Rental houses need a city permit and a county registration.

Lorain at a glance

Lorain has about 65,000 residents, and a little over half of its homes are lived in by their owners. The median owner-occupied home value is $139,200, which is the number most sellers here are pricing against.

The population has held steady since 2020, running 0.2 percent above its April 2020 base.

What buyers like about Lorain

Buyers are drawn by water, parks and an old downtown theater. Lakeview Park is split by West Erie Avenue and has a beach, a bathhouse, picnic shelters and lawn bowling. The city's park department manages 51 parks covering 583 acres, and the lakefront is the part most people point to first.

The Lorain Palace Theatre opened in 1928 and still runs shows. The Lorain International Festival takes place each summer and the Fire Fish Festival each September. These are easy things to mention in a listing or to a buyer who has never lived in town.

Getting around is simple for most households. No interstate runs through the city, so drivers use U.S. Route 6 along Erie Avenue, Ohio 57, and a short stretch of Ohio 2. Lorain County Transit runs two fixed bus lines on Washington Avenue and Broadway toward Elyria. Buyers who care about a particular school should ask the Lorain City School District which building serves your address.

City rules that affect a sale

The Department of Building, Housing and Planning runs several programs that can touch a sale. Its permit page carries forms for rental permits, short-term housing rental licenses, demolition, dumpsters, fences, foundation repair and residential vacant property registration.

Two figures matter most. Vacant property registration costs $125, lasts one year and has to be renewed every year. A $10,000 cash bond must be filed on any property, occupied or not, where a foreclosure case is active or a foreclosure judgment has been entered. The department keeps a form for releasing that bond once the case is resolved.

  • Call the Building Division at 440-204-2045 before you list a vacant house.
  • If tenants ever lived there, ask whether a rental permit is on file.
  • Ask whether a short-term rental license was ever issued for the address.

Sorting these out before you find a buyer keeps surprises away from the closing table. A cash buyer will still ask about them, but they rarely stop a deal when you already have the answers.

How the county auditor handles a transfer

The Lorain County Auditor takes real estate transfers in person or by e-filing, Monday through Thursday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. E-filed transfers stop at 3:00 p.m. and in-person transfers stop at 4:00 p.m. Mailed transfers have not been accepted since November 1, 2012, so plan on a trip or an e-file vendor.

Forms must be typed, since handwritten ones are refused, and a form with missing information or the wrong fee comes back unprocessed. You need only one form per transfer, either a conveyance form or the exemption form. Auditor staff cannot fill in the forms or give legal advice, so a title company or attorney should prepare them. The auditor's transfer rules page links to an e-file vendor list.

Ohio law also requires a statement of value. Under section 319.202, value includes the amount of any mortgage on the property, and willfully falsifying it is prohibited.

Selling a rental house in Lorain County

The buyer has the filing, but you should know about it. State law gives the owner of residential rental property 60 days after the conveyance form is filed to register a contact agent with the county auditor. Missing that window can bring a penalty of up to $150 against the property.

The statute, section 5323.02, covers houses and mobile home park lots with at least one dwelling leased only for residential use. Hotels and dormitories are excluded. Trusts, estates, partnerships, companies and corporations must name a trustee, executor, general partner, member, manager or officer as the contact.

If you sell a rental to an investor, mention the 60-day clock in your contract so nobody is caught out. The auditor also stamps the deed with a reminder when the property is residential rental property.

Property taxes on a Lorain house

Questions about what you owe go to the Lorain County Treasurer at 440-329-5787. Tax amounts are verified and paid through that office. Real estate taxes for 2025 are payable in 2026, and the rates for them were certified on January 7, 2026.

A levy raises a fixed sum of money, so when property values fall the rate has to rise to collect the same amount. That is why a change in your assessed value does not turn into the same percentage change on your bill. The auditor's site also has homestead exemption pages, an owner occupancy reduction page and a conveyance fee calculator.

If taxes are still owed when you sell, they are settled out of the sale proceeds at closing. A title company will show the figure on the settlement statement, and a cash buyer will usually close with the balance handled the same way.

What a cash sale skips in Lorain

Selling for cash removes the steps that most often slow a sale: waiting on a buyer's lender, an appraisal that comes in low, and a repair request after the inspection. You still need a clean title, the transfer forms above, and answers to the city questions about vacancy, foreclosure and rental status.

A practical order of work: confirm whether any city registration or bond applies, ask the treasurer what is owed, gather your mortgage payoff figure if you have one, and have a title company or attorney prepare the conveyance form. With those four things ready, closing can follow whichever date you and the buyer agree on, and you are not tied to an inspection window.

Frequently asked questions

Can a Lorain house with a foreclosure case still be sold?

Yes, but the city requires a $10,000 cash bond on any property with an active foreclosure case or a foreclosure judgment. Ask the Building, Housing and Planning Department how the release form works before you set a closing date.

Does a vacant Lorain house need to be registered?

Ask the Department of Building, Housing and Planning whether your house counts as vacant. The city has a residential vacant property registration form with a $125 fee, valid for one year and renewed annually.

Can I mail my deed to the Lorain County Auditor?

No. Transfers must be delivered in person or through an approved e-file vendor, and mailed conveyances have been refused since November 1, 2012. Manufactured home transfers must be done in person.

What does a buyer of a Lorain rental house have to file?

The buyer files a contact agent form with the county auditor within 60 days after the conveyance form is filed. Missing the window can bring a penalty of up to $150 against the property.

Who helps me prepare the transfer forms?

A title company or attorney. Auditor employees cannot complete conveyance or exemption forms, give legal advice or prepare deeds, because state law bars them from practicing law.

Any sale involves four things: the city's building and planning staff, the short-term rental code if travelers ever stayed in the house, the state disclosure law, and the deed desk at the Butler County Auditor. Each has its own section.

Historic districts and schools

Dayton Lane, German Village and Rossville are the city's three historic districts and hold much of the oldest housing. Anyone changing the outside of a house in one of these districts, or of a listed property, first needs a Certificate of Appropriateness from the Architectural Design Review Board. Say so up front if you are in a district, since a buyer's exterior plans will go through that board.

Hamilton City Schools serve most of the city, and Hamilton High School is the main public high school. A few pockets belong to the Talawanda and Ross Local districts, so verify your street's district before an ad names a school.

Floods have hit the valley for centuries, and the worst came in March 1913. If your parcel is close to the river, find out its flood zone designation from city or county staff.

Permits and city offices

Hamilton's Building Department takes permit applications at building@hamilton-oh.gov and answers questions at (513) 785-7360. The Planning Department, at 513-785-7350, handles zoning, conditional use and variance questions. Electric, plumbing, HVAC, gas and sewer jobs call for a registered contractor. If a past owner did that kind of work, ask the Building Department whether the permit was finished, so a buyer's inspector does not find an open file you did not know about.

The permits page describes a yearly vacant building registration, with a fee that grows each year, aimed at commercial and industrial buildings. A sitting-empty house might be caught by it, so ask first.

Settling an estate often takes a certified death certificate, and the city's Vital Statistics office issues certified birth and death certificates at $25 per copy.

Short-term rental rules

Chapter 758 of the city code governs stays under 30 days. A host needs a license before operating or advertising. If travelers ever stayed in the house, get the license situation straight before listing, because a buyer's agent may raise it.

  • Owner-occupied accessory rentals offer up to two bedrooms with no fee. Large and commercial rentals pay $50.
  • A license runs for two years, with renewal due 30 days in advance.
  • An emergency contact must respond within 24 hours, and utilities must be current.
  • Penalties escalate from a letter to a $250 fine, then $500 plus a six-month suspension, and finally revocation with fines that can reach $1,000 daily.

The city's permits page links each application.

When can a Hamilton seller skip Ohio's disclosure form?

Estates and rentals feed a lot of Hamilton sales, which is why the exceptions in R.C. 5302.30 matter here. A seller acting for someone else, such as an executor, guardian or trustee, does not have to hand over the form. Neither does an heir who inherited the house and did not live in it during the past year. Court-ordered sales, foreclosure sales and deeds in lieu of foreclosure also fall outside the rule.

An investor who bought a rental and never lived in it fits none of those categories. Having tenants in the house changes nothing, so that seller still owes the buyer a completed form. The statute lists each category, and a title agent can say which one fits you.

Butler County Auditor and the deed

The Auditor's Conveyance Department handles every ownership change in Butler County and collects the fees. The conveyance fee works out to $.30 for each $100 of price, or $3 per $1,000, with the price rounded up to the next $100 first. Each parcel adds $0.50.

  • Payment must be cash or a check made out to the Butler County Auditor.
  • Staff cannot make change, and they will not complete a blank check.
  • On a residential rental, the Auditor's endorsement reminds the buyer to file landlord information under R.C. 5323.02.

The deed transfer page has the forms. The title company usually carries the deed in. Have it confirm how to pay before closing day.

When does a quick cash sale suit a Hamilton owner?

Direct sales make sense when repairs would cost more than the house can bear, when tenants are living there, or when an estate has a deadline. Put a written cash offer next to what a repaired listing would net after contractor bills, commissions and months of carrying costs.

Listing with an agent fits a house in decent shape on a street where owner-occupants shop. A cash buyer needs no loan approval and takes the house as it stands, so repairs and showings drop out. Have each buyer write down the price, the closing date and who pays which cost.

At Hamilton's price levels, even modest repair bills eat a noticeable slice of the sale, and that is why owners of dated houses often check direct offers first.

From offer to closing

This sequence suits most sales here, whether an investor or a family is buying.

  1. Ask the city or county about the parcel's flood zone and any historic district.
  2. Phone the Building Department about permits from earlier work, and Planning about zoning.
  3. For a former short-term rental, settle the license question.
  4. Work out whether the disclosure form applies. Estate fiduciaries and absentee heirs are often exempt.
  5. Pull together the lease and tenant details when the house is rented, because the buyer files landlord information with the Auditor.
  6. Let the title company draft the deed and bring the exact fee as cash or a check to the Butler County Auditor.

Finally, get the closing date, the split of title and recording costs, and the buyer's plan if a walkthrough turns up a surprise, all in writing.

Do I need a permit to run a vacation rental in Hamilton?

Yes, you need a Short-Term Rental License before running or advertising stays under 30 days. Owner-occupied rentals of up to two bedrooms pay no fee, while large or commercial ones pay $50.

How is the Butler County deed fee figured?

The fee is $.30 per $100 of price, which is $3 per $1,000, after rounding up to the next $100. Each parcel adds $0.50. Cash or a check to the Butler County Auditor settles it.

Does an inherited Hamilton house need the state condition form?

Frequently not. Under R.C. 5302.30, an estate fiduciary or an heir who stayed out of the house the previous year is exempt. Ask a title agent about your facts.

Which school district serves my Hamilton street?

Hamilton City Schools cover most addresses, though a few fall in Talawanda or Ross Local. The district can look up your address.

Do historic district rules limit what a Hamilton buyer can change?

They can. Exterior work in a district needs Certificate of Appropriateness approval from the Architectural Design Review Board. The districts are Dayton Lane, German Village and Rossville.
