Selling a house in Youngstown

Youngstown, the Mahoning County seat, has an estimated 58,832 residents. That's down 2.0% from the 60,049 counted in 2020 and well below the 66,982 counted in 2010. The city grew around coal, iron and steel mills along the Mahoning River, and the effects show in a smaller population than the city was built for and a lot of older housing. The county auditor's office, the courthouse and most of the records you need for a sale are in the city.

Home values and incomes

Prices here sit at a very different scale than most of Ohio. The 2020 to 2024 median home value is $63,300 and median rent is $728, with 56.2% of the city's 24,982 households owning. Median household income is $34,408.

  • Monthly owner costs run $916 with a mortgage and $379 without.
  • Youngstown State University, with about 11,000 students, is the largest employer in the city.
  • Health care is the biggest economic sector.

At values this low, a repair bill can swallow much of the price. Buyers and investors count every roof and plumbing problem, so know your house's condition before you set an asking price.

Neighborhoods buyers ask about

Downtown holds government buildings, banks and venues such as the Covelli Centre and Powers Auditorium, with Youngstown State University and the Butler Institute of American Art just to the north. The North Side includes Brier Hill, Crandall Park, North Heights and Wick Park, where industrial executives built mansions that still stand in historic districts. The South Side is the densest part of the city and includes Oak Hill, Erie, Warren and Lower Gibson.

Interstate 680 serves the city directly and connects to I-80, the Ohio Turnpike and State Route 11. State Route 711 runs north, and the Madison Avenue and Himrod Avenue expressways form a freeway loop around downtown. The Youngstown City School District covers almost all of the city.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Youngstown house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Rental and vacant property registration

Registration is the Youngstown rule that surprises sellers most. Under Section 546.11 of the city's Codified Ordinances, every rental property must be registered and hold a city license renewed annually, other than public housing and Section 8 units, which follow federal inspection rules. Except for owner-occupied homes, all properties must now be registered.

  • The fee is $40 for a single rental unit. In a multi-unit building it is $40 for the first unit and $25 for each additional unit.
  • An unlicensed rental can be fined $100 for each week it is unlicensed, and criminal penalties are possible.
  • Once the form and fee arrive, a provisional license is issued for one year while an inspection is scheduled within 30 days.
  • If the property fails inspection the owner has 30 days to fix the violations, and each re-inspection costs $40.
  • Cancelling an inspection after 8:00 a.m. on the day costs $25, and later late cancellations cost $100 each.

Vacant properties have their own registration program run by the same office. Before you list a vacant house, call the Property Registration Department at (330) 742-8743 and ask whether the address is registered and whether fees are open. The office keeps weekday hours from 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.

A house on the demolition list

Youngstown decides which houses are condemned, so ask the city first. Call the Property Code Enforcement and Demolition office at (330) 742-8888 to find out where an address stands. The Mahoning County Land Bank acts at the request of cities, villages and townships when demolition funds are available.

The Land Bank answers a few questions that come up in sales. It owns no houses for renovation. It holds no owner phone numbers, so a buyer must find the deeded owner through the auditor's property search. And buying a house for $1 is an urban legend.

If a house is torn down, taxes still follow the building for a time. Taxes are collected a year behind, so you're still taxed on the building's value if it was standing on January 1 of the tax year being collected. A demolition permit for a Youngstown residence comes from the city's Property Code Enforcement and Demolition Department.

Mahoning County values and appeals

Ohio requires each county auditor to reappraise every parcel every six years. Mahoning County completed its reappraisal for tax year 2023, with taxes collected in 2024, and the next reappraisal is for tax year 2030. A triennial update, which studies sales without visiting each property, applies to tax year 2026 with taxes collected in 2027.

Owners who think the county's number is high file a Complaint Against the Valuation of Real Property, accepted from January 2 through March 31. Three officers sit on the Board of Revision, the auditor, the treasurer and the commissioners' president, and the hearing covers value only. Its address is 120 Market Street in Youngstown, and the auditor's office can be reached at (330) 740-2010. For payment questions, call the county treasurer at (330) 740-2460.

Evidence the Mahoning Board of Revision accepts for residential value complaints
EvidenceWhat to submit
Recent saleClosing statement, purchase agreement and conveyance statement for a sale within 24 months, with a notarized arm's-length affidavit
ListingA listing agreement if the property is currently for sale
AppraisalA report by a certified appraiser for tax valuation, subject to review
ConditionPhotographs with professional repair estimates
New constructionBuilder-certified costs for work five years old or less

A tax increase by itself isn't a ground for a value complaint, because taxes result from voted levies.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Youngstown houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Ohio disclosure form

The state disclosure form under Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 covers most one to four unit sales, with carve-outs for foreclosure sales, deeds in lieu, court-ordered transfers and estate fiduciaries. Anyone selling in one of those roles should confirm which carve-out applies.

The city also publishes a Property Transfer Affidavit, among the forms on its code enforcement page. Ask the Property Code Enforcement and Demolition office whether your sale needs one before you set a closing.

When a cash offer makes sense

A cash offer makes sense when the cost of repair, a rental license problem or a vacant-property registration issue would hold up a conventional buyer's financing. A lender's appraiser and inspector will look closely at a house with roof, plumbing or foundation problems, and the low values here leave little cushion.

Compare more than one offer, ask who pays closing costs, and get the closing date in writing. Request the settlement statement early and check that any unpaid city fees or taxes come out of your proceeds.

Steps before you close

Begin by finding out how the city sees your address. Call the Property Registration Department about rental or vacant registration, and the Property Code Enforcement and Demolition office about any condemnation or demolition status. Fix or settle open fees so they don't surface at the title search.

Next, handle the county side. Confirm with the treasurer what is owed, and decide whether you want to file a value complaint during the January 2 to March 31 window. If you've lived in the house and are selling as an heir or fiduciary, check which disclosure carve-out applies.

Last, choose how to sell. An as-is buyer may close sooner and skips the appraisal, but registration, taxes and the disclosure rules still apply. Check that city fees and unpaid taxes come out of your proceeds on the settlement statement.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Do I have to register a rental before I sell a Youngstown house?

If the house is rented, it must be registered and hold a city license each year, and an unlicensed rental can be fined $100 for each week. Call the Property Registration Department at (330) 742-8743 to confirm the status of your address before closing.

What if my Youngstown house is vacant and on the demolition list?

Call the Property Code Enforcement and Demolition office at (330) 742-8888. Local governments decide which houses are condemned, and the Mahoning County Land Bank acts on their requests when funding is available.

When do I file a value complaint in Mahoning County?

File between January 2 and March 31. Complaints for tax year 2026 begin January 2, 2027, and mail or in-person filing goes to the Board of Revision at 120 Market Street.

Is there a disclosure exemption for estate sales in Youngstown?

Yes. The disclosure statute excuses an estate fiduciary, and it also excuses transfers made by court order.

Will I still pay tax on a Youngstown house I demolish?

Yes for the year in question. Taxes are collected a year behind, so a building standing on the January 1 tax date is still taxed that year.

Springfield's housing market for sellers

Prices run low in Springfield and renters are common, which decides who shows up to buy. The typical owned home is worth $116,800 and the typical rent is $851. Owners hold 52.4% of the 24,650 households, and the median household earns $47,143. Springfield is the Clark County seat, roughly 45 miles west of Columbus and 25 miles northeast of Dayton. Headcount fell from 60,608 in 2010 to 58,662 in 2020, and the July 2025 estimate is 58,281.

Many buyers are investors planning to rent, so expect offers built around rental income and repair cost.

Older houses from the factory years

A lot of the housing goes back to the Champion City era, when factories employed much of the town. Population topped 82,000 in the 1960 census. Factory jobs then shrank and left many blocks of aging frame houses, so weigh repair spending against a modest sale price.

Some pockets are historic, such as the South Fountain Avenue Historic District and the Frank Lloyd Wright-designed Westcott House on East High Street. Houses nearby can attract a different kind of buyer, and it pays to ask the city before changing the outside of a house on a historic street.

Rental property registry

Nearly half of Springfield households rent, and the city keeps a Rental Property Registry for those units. If you have a tenant, make sure your registration is current and this year's fee is paid before the house goes on the market.

Springfield rental registry fees
Rental typeAnnual registry fee
Single unit property$35
Two or more units in one building$25 per unit
Cap per owner and per LLC$750

Finishing a rental registration does not currently require the self-inspection checklist. Call 937-324-7385 with questions, and register through the online portal called City Works Online. Hold on to the receipt, since a buyer may want proof.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Springfield house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Vacant property registry

A separate Vacant Property Registry runs through HERA Property Registry. For an empty house, the city's Responsible Property Programming office can say if you must register and what it costs.

Visit 76 E. High Street, second floor, between 8 and 5. Complaints about an empty house tend to follow it into a sale, because boarded windows, tall grass or failing systems show up quickly in an inspection. That is one reason owners of vacant houses consider an as-is sale.

Which school district is your address in?

Springfield City Schools cover most addresses. The Northeastern and Northwestern local districts take parts of the north, and Clark-Shawnee Local takes parts of the west, south and southeast. Confirm the district for your exact address before advertising it.

Clark County tax installments

Clark County collects in two installments. Pay an installment late and a 5% penalty applies, climbing to 10% after a short window. The Treasurer, 937-521-1832, has current due dates and the balance for your parcel.

Bills go out 20 to 25 days before the due date, and a missing bill is no excuse for a late payment. An escrow program lets owners prepay monthly. At closing your title agent prorates the bill by days of ownership, so request that figure early.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Springfield houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Recording a deed in Clark County

R.C. 5301.25 sends a deed to the county where the land sits. The auditor indorses it after the grantee files a statement of value (R.C. 319.202), and the grantor pays the conveyance fee. On a residential rental, the indorsement also tells the grantee to file landlord details with the auditor, something investor buyers should expect.

Mention the Rental Property Registry to a rental buyer early. If they intend to keep renting, they will register under their own name after closing, and a clean record makes that easy.

Selling a house with a tenant in it

Locate your registry receipt and confirm the current year is paid. Next, agree with the buyer on whether the tenant stays. An investor may welcome the lease, but an owner-occupant will want a move-out date in the contract. Share the lease and rent history at the outset. When title changes, the new owner registers the property, and the deed indorsement points them to the auditor's landlord filing.

Selling a vacant house

Neighbors and inspectors notice an empty house. Ask the Responsible Property Programming office whether the address is on the Vacant Property Registry and whether complaints are open. Deal with what shows from the street first. If the problems go deeper than looks, an as-is buyer can spare you months of carrying costs. Leave utilities connected through the inspection, and have your title agent confirm no city charge is attached to the parcel.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Steps for a Springfield sale

  1. Pull the parcel number and call the Treasurer to learn what is owed and when the next installment is due.
  2. Check city records for rental or vacant registration and any open code item.
  3. Choose a route: agent listing, sale on your own, or direct cash buyer.
  4. Sign a contract and let the title agent run the search.
  5. Have the deed and statement of value prepared, with the conveyance fee set aside from your proceeds.
  6. Review the settlement statement, including the tax proration, before you sign.

Questions for your title agent

Bring a short list to the first call. Which county office will record the deed, and what will the conveyance fee come to on your price? Does the search show a rental or vacant registration, an unpaid tax installment or a city charge on the parcel? How will the tax bill be prorated, and will the statement of value be filed by the buyer or by the agent? If you hold a tenant's lease, ask whether it needs to be attached to the contract. Written answers are best, since you can hand them to any buyer who asks and compare offers on equal terms.

At a median value near $116,800, small costs matter more than they would in a pricier market. A registry fee, a repair bill and closing charges can add up against the sale price, so ask for every number before you accept an offer.

Is a cash sale the right fit?

It can be, if repairs would eat the gain from a retail listing. With a median value of $116,800, one big job such as a roof or furnace weighs heavily against the price, and a financed buyer may insist you do it first.

A direct buyer typically purchases as is, which suits a vacant or tenant-occupied house with open code items. Get two written offers, ask who covers closing costs, and review the settlement statement before the closing date.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a city inspection before a Springfield house can be sold?

Ask the city's Responsible Property Programming office at 76 E. High Street whether your address has open code items or a vacant registration. Springfield's rental and vacant registries are the main property rules that touch a sale.

How much does Springfield charge to register a rental?

The annual fee is $35 for a single unit and $25 per unit in a building with two or more units, capped at $750 per owner and per LLC. Call 937-324-7385 with questions.

What is the late penalty on a Clark County tax bill?

An unpaid half draws a 5% penalty, which rises to 10% after a short grace window. Call the Treasurer at 937-521-1832 for the dates that apply.

Who pays the conveyance fee on a Springfield sale?

Under R.C. 319.202 the seller pays the fee, plus any county transfer tax the county has levied. The title company can quote the exact amount.

Which Springfield neighborhoods are historic?

The South Fountain Avenue Historic District is one, and the Westcott House on East High Street was designed by Frank Lloyd Wright. Check with the city before planning exterior changes on a historic street.

Which sale path suits a Kettering house best?

A Kettering owner who wants top dollar and has time should list with an agent, while an owner facing a deadline, heavy repairs or an estate usually gets further with a cash buyer. Selling alone sits in between, since the commission stays with you along with every task.

Kettering had 57,396 residents in mid 2025, a dip of less than one percent from 2020. The city filled in during the 1950s and 1960s and has plenty of postwar houses, so buyers often ask about wiring, plumbing and windows.

With nearly one in five residents 65 or older, expect long held houses and estate sales to make up a fair share of what comes to market.

Schools and neighborhood context

Kettering is served by the Kettering City School District, which includes Kettering Fairmont High School. Use the district name accurately in a listing and point buyers to the district office for attendance questions, since city and district boundaries can differ.

The city counts 20 parks, the Fraze Pavilion concert venue, Rosewood Arts Center and Pondview Park's nature trails. The Greater Dayton Regional Transit Authority runs buses, and the typical worker spends about 20.3 minutes getting to work. Permits and property maintenance

Kettering reviews construction through its Planning and Development Department, reachable at 937-296-2441. Under Ordinance 1301, a project needs approval from every city department that applies, whether building, fire, zoning or stormwater, before work starts. The city aims to finish reviews in 10 days and says it can take up to 30 when demand is high.

  • Certificate of Occupancy: issued only after the required inspections pass and every department signs off.
  • Finished work: if you added a deck, finished a basement or replaced a furnace, locate the permit and final inspection record before you list.
  • Rental condition: the city's landlord and tenant guide requires an owner to keep mechanical, electrical and plumbing systems up to code, heating able to hold 68 degrees, and water heating at no less than 110 degrees at the taps.

A structure that fails the code can be condemned and posted as unfit for human habitation, so cure visible violations early. A rental seller can also point the buyer to the same guide to show what was maintained.

How is a deed transferred in Montgomery County?

Because Kettering sits in Montgomery County, the County Auditor processes the deed transfer, and this step is needed for the transfer to count as a legal transaction. The conveyance fee is $3 per $1,000 of the actual sale price plus $.50 for each parcel. Call 937-225-4373 with questions. Filers can also use ePN or Simplifile for electronic submission.

Ohio Revised Code 319.202 requires the buyer's side to file a statement declaring the property's value, and it puts the fee on the seller. A seller who has claimed a property tax reduction should expect to answer a question about it on that statement.

Ohio's disclosure form for Kettering sellers

Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 covers the disclosure form for one to four unit homes. It lists exceptions such as transfers by court order, by an executor or other fiduciary, and between spouses or parents and children. Most arm's length sales of a Kettering house do need the form.

Selling as is does not change that. A house with an old furnace or dated wiring can sell, but you still answer the form honestly about problems you know of. Cash buyers price the repair in, while financed buyers may ask you to fix it.

Is a cash offer the right call for a Kettering owner?

Take a cash offer when the sale must follow your timetable and the house would struggle in a conventional listing. Examples include a worn mid century home, a property with a code citation still open, or an estate whose heirs live elsewhere.

Get every offer in writing and weigh it against what an agent would likely net after commission, repairs and carrying costs. Settle who pays title and recording fees plus the Montgomery County transfer charge, and keep your own copy of the disclosure form and any permit records for the buyer.

Ask what the buyer does if a walkthrough finds something new, and get the closing date in writing. A firm date matters most when you are paying for a second household or carrying an empty house.

Before you list or sign

Some homework up front prevents problems at the closing table.

  1. Pull permit records for any deck, basement finish or furnace replacement, and ask the Planning and Development Department whether the final inspection passed.
  2. Walk the house for visible code problems and fix them, because a failed structure can be condemned.
  3. If you rent the house, gather the lease and the maintenance records that show heat, water heating and wiring were kept up.
  4. Fill out the disclosure form and keep a signed copy.
  5. Ask the title company to confirm the Montgomery County charge so it shows on the settlement statement.

A cash sale compresses this list into a few days, but the permit records and the disclosure form are still yours to supply, and any serious buyer will ask for them. If heirs live elsewhere, one person with authority to sign should collect the papers and be the contact for the title company. Keeping everything in one folder, paper or digital, makes it easy to hand the buyer a complete record on request.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Montgomery County transfer charge on a Kettering sale?

The conveyance fee is $3 per $1,000 of the actual sale price plus $.50 per parcel. Under Ohio Revised Code 319.202 the seller bears that charge, and it should show on the settlement statement.

Will a buyer ask for permit records on a Kettering house?

Buyers and lenders sometimes ask for one. Kettering's Planning and Development Department at 937-296-2441 can tell you what was permitted and whether a final inspection was passed.

Can a Kettering house sell with an outdated furnace or wiring?

Yes, a house can sell as is, but the seller still completes the Ohio disclosure form under Revised Code 5302.30 and answers honestly about known problems. Cash buyers price the repair in, while financed buyers may ask the seller to fix it.

Which school district do Kettering addresses belong to?

Most addresses are in the Kettering City School District, whose high school is Kettering Fairmont. City and district boundaries can differ, so a buyer should verify a particular address with the district office.

Who handles property maintenance complaints about a Kettering rental?

The city's Planning and Development Department answers questions about the code at 937-296-2441. The landlord guide on the city site lists the standards for walls, hallways, plumbing, heating and wiring that owners must meet.

Choosing how to sell in Elyria

Speed in Elyria usually comes from a cash buyer, because no mortgage underwriting stands between you and closing. Listing with an agent exposes the house to more shoppers, yet you wait on appraisals and loan approvals. Selling alone saves a fee and hands you every chore.

  • Agent listing: suits a house in good shape when your calendar allows for a lender's timeline.

Many Lorain County houses went up for factory workers generations ago, and their roofs, boilers and wiring show it. A lender's inspector writes those items up. A cash buyer simply subtracts them from the offer at the start.

Elyria housing at a glance

Elyria, the Lorain County seat, counts 53,634 residents for July 2025, up from 52,656 in 2020, across roughly 20.8 square miles. The median owner-occupied home is valued at $156,100, and owners live in 60.0 percent of homes. There were 24,904 housing units in 2020, with 7.8 percent vacant. About 35.5 percent of the 22,954 households are one person.

Renters pay a median $906, and median household income is $54,945. At those rents, a lot of shoppers are first-time buyers or investors comparing a purchase to rental income. A signed lease attracts the investor and can put off the first-time buyer, so decide which of the two you want before you market the house.

Offices to call before closing

Your first call goes to the Building Department, 131 Court Street, Suite 101, at 440-326-1491. It issues permits, applies the Ohio residential code and the city's codified ordinances, and looks into property maintenance complaints. Ask whether any permit at your address remains open. Unfinished work stalls more closings than anything else on this list.

  • West by the River district: exterior repairs, replacements and additions to homes here need Landmarks Preservation Commission approval. Interiors and gardens don't.
  • Rental registration: the permits page has a Rental Unit Registration Form. A landlord who is selling should verify the registration is current.
  • Accessory structures: sheds, fences and pools use the zoning permit application. A missing one can turn up during a buyer's inspection.
  • Utilities: the office at 440-326-1570 sets up water, sewer and sanitation accounts. Give it your sale date.
  • Regional income tax: the city homepage links to RITA for filing and paying, which matters if you leave the city.

A packet with a wrong fee or a blank line is returned, and staff hold nothing for later. Ohio Revised Code section 4705.01 bars the Auditor's staff from completing forms or advising on deeds, which is why a title company or attorney usually drafts them.

The state disclosure form

Ohio Revised Code section 5302.30 requires owners of one to four unit residential property to give prospective buyers a signed disclosure form. Exceptions include transfers by an estate fiduciary and sales by an heir who never lived in the home.

Selling as is doesn't waive the form. It only signals that you won't be paying for repairs the buyer discovers. Answer the form accurately and attach receipts where you have them, because a vague answer usually brings more questions from the buyer than a plain one.

When cash is the better fit

Certainty can outweigh price. A roof about to fail, a basement that floods, a tenant who refuses to leave, a relative's estate or a lender's deadline are the usual reasons Elyria owners choose cash.

Gather two or three offers, and ask to see proof of funds. Then phone the Lorain County Auditor's real estate department to learn the conveyance fee, so your closing statement has no surprises.

Once you've accepted an offer, the title company searches the record and requests a payoff figure from any lender holding a mortgage. In parallel, ask the Building Department about open permits, and give the Utilities office your sale date so the accounts transfer cleanly.

At the signing you execute the deed and the matching conveyance or exemption form. The title company carries the finished packet to the Auditor ahead of the cutoff. Take photo identification. If tenants live in the house, take the lease and their contact details. If you're selling an inherited property, take whatever proves you hold authority to sell.

Without a lender's appraisal, a cash purchase can close sooner. The documents are the same either way, so settle in writing who pays each charge before you agree to the price.

Paperwork to gather first

Pull your deed, the latest property tax bill, receipts for roof, furnace and electrical work, and any permit records for sheds, fences or pools. If the house sits in the West by the River district, add the Landmarks Preservation Commission approvals for exterior changes. Buyers and title agents ask for these in roughly the same order, so a ready folder keeps the contract moving.

Also confirm every owner's name on the deed matches your identification. A mismatch, or a missing co-owner, is the kind of small gap that gets a packet sent back from the Auditor on closing day.

Selling an Elyria rental with tenants inside

A tenant living in the house does not block a sale. Start with the lease: note the end date and the notice terms, and tell prospective buyers about the tenancy at the first conversation. An investor may want to keep the tenant, while an owner-occupant buyer will need the house empty, and that difference decides who can realistically close on your timeline.

Check that your city rental registration is current before you list, since an out-of-date registration is easy to fix now and annoying to discover at closing. Put the lease, rent ledger and any repair requests in the folder you hand to buyers.

Can I sell an Elyria house without fixing anything?

Yes, selling as is is common. You still owe buyers the Ohio disclosure form when Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 covers the sale. Lender-backed buyers may request repairs after inspecting, while a cash buyer usually subtracts the cost from the price.

Who handles code complaints and open permits for an address in Elyria?

The Building Department at 440-326-1491. Staff can say whether permits remain open and whether complaints are on file.

Which office records the transfer of an Elyria property?

The Lorain County Auditor, in person or through an approved e-filing vendor. Mailed real estate transfers aren't accepted.

May I sell Elyria rental property with a tenant living in it?

Yes. Read the lease for its end date and notice terms, tell buyers early, and confirm your city rental registration is current.

What does an owner-occupied home usually sell for in Elyria?

The median value is $156,100. Your own figure depends on condition, street and size, so compare recent sales nearby.

How a sale works in Middletown

Middletown lies along the Great Miami River, roughly 29 miles northeast of Cincinnati and 20 miles southwest of Dayton, and it straddles two counties. Older houses from the steel years

Middletown grew around paper, farming and, from 1900, a sheet steel plant that still runs as part of Cleveland-Cliffs. Schools and transit

Anywhere in the Butler County part of Middletown, students belong to the Middletown City School District, which operates Middletown High School. The Warren County part is divided among the Middletown City, Franklin City and Lebanon City districts, so confirm the district for the address before writing a listing.

Buses from the Butler County Regional Transit Authority link to Hamilton, Oxford and Springdale, where riders can switch to the Cincinnati regional system. Families often ask about districts early, so have the answer ready.

Property standards that can come up

Development Services publishes a maintenance sheet that draws on the International Property Maintenance Code and local ordinances. A buyer's agent or city inspector may point to these items:

  • Grass and weeds: kept under 6 inches, and cut within 5 days of a city notice (Ordinance 678).
  • Junk vehicles: a non-running vehicle left uncovered more than 7 days after notice breaks the rules (Ordinance 660.07).
  • Furniture, mattresses and appliances outside: not allowed in a yard or on an open porch for more than 48 hours (Ordinance 660.21).
  • Windows: broken glass must be repaired, and screens are required on windows.
  • Pools and hot tubs: a pool or spa holding more than 24 inches of water needs a surrounding barrier of at least 48 inches, with a gate that closes and latches itself.
  • Trees: branches must clear 12 feet over the street and 9 feet over the sidewalk.
  • Sidewalks: the owner keeps them in good repair and free of snow, ice and leaves.

Ask Code Enforcement if the address has open notices. A nuisance abatement or unpaid mowing charge is easier to resolve before closing than afterward.

Butler County deed transfers

Deed copies sit with the Recorder. A parcel in the Warren County part of town follows Warren County's schedule instead, so ask that auditor for its fees and steps. State law (R.C. 322.02) caps a county transfer tax at thirty cents per hundred dollars.

The auditor also has a tool that shows each levy by taxing district for any parcel. Open the Current Tax Distribution tab on your parcel, and note that the totals there are calculated before rollbacks such as the owner-occupancy credit or homestead exemption, so the figures run higher than your bill. Ask the auditor how a sale in the current year affects credits the next owner can claim.

Inherited and rental houses

Ohio's disclosure statute (R.C. 5302.30) exempts some transfers from the seller form, such as sales by an estate fiduciary and sales by an heir who has not occupied the home for a year. A buyer will still ask about the roof, sewer line and water damage, so answer honestly and in writing.

For a tenant-occupied house, landlord and tenant disputes are filed in the civil division of Middletown Municipal Court. The filing fee is $115 for one defendant and $20 for each added defendant, with a $15,000 ceiling on damages or counterclaims. An owner that is not an individual needs an attorney. When the deed is endorsed on a residential rental property, the auditor's endorsement reminds the buyer to make the county rental property filing under R.C. 5323.02.

When a cash offer makes sense

With a midpoint value near $164,400 and many older houses, repair costs can eat a large part of the sale price. A direct sale can suit a house that needs a roof, a vacant property with code notices, or an estate whose heirs live far away.

Getting ready to close

Find out first which county your parcel sits in, since that sets the auditor, the fees and the school district. Then walk the property against the maintenance list above and clear anything outdoors that a code officer would flag. Order a payoff letter if you owe on a mortgage, and have an attorney or title company prepare the deed with a legal description the engineer's office can approve. The buyer files the value or exemption statement, you pay the transfer charge when the deed is presented, and the recorder holds the copy. A cash buyer works through the same steps without a lender's schedule.

Which county handles my Middletown deed?

That depends on where the parcel sits. Butler County covers most of the city and Warren County a portion. Check the parcel on a county auditor's property search to see who processes the transfer.

What is the Butler County conveyance fee?

Butler County's auditor posts $3 per thousand of price, with the price rounded up to a full hundred, and $.50 per parcel, payable by cash or check.

How high can my grass be in Middletown?

Keep it under 6 inches. After a city notice the owner has 5 days to cut. Confirm current wording with Code Enforcement before you list.

What is Middletown's median home value?

The midpoint for owned homes is $164,400. A particular house can sit far from that, depending on size, age and repair needs.

Can I sell a Middletown house with tenants in it?

Yes. A sale does not cancel a lease on its own, so give the buyer the lease terms and deposit details. Cases that need an eviction go to Middletown Municipal Court.

  • Clear gutters and downspouts and look for water lines on basement walls before showing the house.
  • Check porch posts and concrete steps for freeze damage.
  • Note the age of the furnace, water heater and roof, since inspectors record each one.

Small repairs made early can matter more than fresh paint, because an inspection report hands the buyer a list to negotiate from.

Homes in older neighborhoods may fall in a historic area, such as the Hudson Avenue Historic District. Collect permits, receipts for roof or furnace work and renovation notes, because buyers ask for them before they offer.

Offices and permits before you list

Property maintenance enforcement belongs to the Department of Public Safety. Code 07-03 follows the International Property Maintenance Code, modified for Newark. Complaints go to the division by email or phone, and in-person visits are by appointment.

The Division of Zoning, at 40 W. Main Street, issues permits under a fee schedule. A few entries bear on a sale or a cleanout:

Should it arrive after an offer is made, the buyer holds a three business day right to cancel in writing, which expires at the earlier of 30 days post-acceptance or closing.

A signed form given before the offer removes that rescission option. The statute carves out exemptions, such as sales by an estate fiduciary, and allows a buyer to waive the cancellation right, so read contract wording closely.

Tax values and relief programs

Licking County's auditor values property for tax purposes and transfers deeds, and also serves as secretary to the Board of Revision and the Budget Commission. The same office runs the tax reduction programs. An owner currently receiving a reduction should tell the buyer and title company, since the next owner has to qualify separately.

Steps from accepted offer to recorded deed

After you accept an offer, have a title company or attorney prepare the deed. Sign it before a notary, and make sure the buyer's side completes the value statement. Your mortgage payoff and any unpaid property tax come out of the proceeds, and the treasurer can tell you whether a balance remains. Ask for the settlement statement early and compare it with the offer. A cash buyer skips the lender's appraisal and timeline, so you can often pick a closing day that fits your move. Before the closing appointment, clear out belongings you are not leaving, turn off or transfer utilities for the closing date, and bring photo identification for the notary. Walk through the house one last time and take date-stamped photos of its condition. Keep a copy of the recorded deed and the final settlement statement with your tax records.

How can I report a code problem in Newark?

Email or call the Division of Property Maintenance Enforcement. It enforces Code 07-03, which is built on the International Property Maintenance Code.

Most owners selling one to four unit homes complete the state property disclosure form (R.C. 5302.30) and give each prospective buyer a signed copy. If the form comes late, the buyer has three business days after getting it to cancel.

How a Cuyahoga Falls sale works

Most owners hire a listing agent, though some handle the sale alone or deal with a buyer who closes on the house in its present condition. Each route ends at the same desks in Summit County. Buyer and seller sign the city's stormwater disclosure, someone prepares a deed, and the county Fiscal Office transfers and records it. The routes differ in how long the wait runs, who pays for repairs, and how much uncertainty the seller absorbs.

Cuyahoga Falls lies directly north of Akron and is the second-largest city in Summit County. It has 25.80 square miles of land, 51,114 residents in the 2020 count and an estimate of 50,975 for July 2025, a slip of 0.2 percent that describes a settled city.

The city's past and today's houses

A river power town became a residential suburb, and that history explains both the street pattern and the school boundaries. Settlers dammed the Cuyahoga River in 1812 to run mills, and by the middle of the twentieth century the mills had faded and the city was mostly homes.

Census tallies show the speed of the change: 20,546 residents in 1940, then 47,922 by 1960. A house from those decades invites buyer questions about sewer laterals, gutters and downspouts, the very items the city's stormwater inspection examines.

In 1986 the city merged with Northampton Township, the first merger of a city and a township in Ohio. The former township land lies in the northwest and kept its own school district, so describe a northwest property by the right district name.

Cuyahoga Falls homes by the numbers

Owners hold a majority here. A typical owner-occupied home is valued at $183,300, and 64.4 percent of the city's 23,212 households own their homes. These are 2020 through 2024 figures.

  • Renters pay a median gross rent of $1,038 a month.
  • Owners with a mortgage report median monthly costs of $1,349; those without one report $578.
  • Median household income is $72,705, and the average commute takes 21.6 minutes.
  • The 2020 Census counted 24,827 housing units, 5.7 percent of them vacant.

The homeowner vacancy rate was only 1.1 percent in 2020, so an owner-occupied house that needs work often sits beside tidier listings aimed at the same buyers.

Four school districts reach into the city

The Cuyahoga Falls City School District covers nearly all of the original city area, with its high school near downtown, and it also takes in the village of Silver Lake.

The former Northampton Township area is served by Woodridge Local School District, whose high school is in Cuyahoga Falls even though its mailing address says Peninsula. A small slice of the northeast is zoned to Hudson City School District, and a sliver of the far northwest is in Revere Local School District. Verify the district for your parcel before a listing names one.

Stormwater inspection at sale

The city offers a free stormwater inspection, and every house sale there needs the buyer and the seller to sign off on the related disclosure. The inspection looks for clean water getting into the sanitary sewer from private property, such as downspouts or footer drains tied to the wrong pipe. Anything that violates city code must be repaired within 180 days after the inspection.

Chapter 1306 of the city's codified ordinances sets the mechanics:

  • The owner, or a buyer under contract, may ask the city to inspect sewer laterals, sewer connections, gutters, downspouts and footer drains.
  • The city does the work at its own cost and may use a sewer camera, smoke or dye testing.
  • A Certificate of Inspection reaches the owner within ten days, and the requesting buyer too when a buyer asked.
  • Once an owner holds a certificate, the purchaser must receive a copy before any transfer.
  • After repairs, the owner can request a Certificate of Completion.

The same chapter bars anyone from selling sewer-served property without telling the buyer the inspection exists, on a form from the City Engineer. Breaking the chapter is a fourth-degree misdemeanor. Request forms sit in the housing and development section of the city's permits page.

Open code problems on your house

The city's housing division enforces property maintenance and zoning rules through inspections and complaint investigations. Complaints can be made anonymously, and each one is tracked. The development department takes calls at (330) 971-8135.

The most frequent violations are:

  • overgrown weeds, trees or shrubbery in the yard;
  • trash and refuse left outside;
  • abandoned or inoperable vehicles, boats and trailers;
  • garages, sheds, fences or houses in poor structural repair;
  • pet waste left on the ground.

Mowing a yard or hauling off a derelict trailer costs far less than negotiating around it after a buyer's walk-through. An inherited house that has stood empty is a common place for these items to pile up.

Ohio's disclosure statute

Section 5302.30 of the Ohio Revised Code applies to residential property with one to four units. The owner fills out the state form and delivers a signed copy to the buyer promptly. If the form first arrives after a contract exists, the buyer gets three business days from receipt to cancel in writing, and the right ends at thirty days after acceptance or at closing, whichever comes first.

Some transfers fall outside the rule, including court-ordered sales and sales by an estate's fiduciary. An heir who took the house by inheritance and never lived in it during the prior year is also exempt, which describes many Summit County estate sales.

Summit County transfer and recording charges

The Fiscal Office charges a transfer fee and a separate recording fee on every sale.

Summit County Fiscal Office charges for a sale
ChargeRate
Conveyance fee$4.00 per $1000, with the sale price rounded up to the next $100
Lot fee50 cents for each lot named in the legal description
Recording a deed$34 covers two pages; each added page costs $8
Copy of a recorded deed$4, and $1 more for a certified copy
Recording turnaround3 to 5 working days

The recording division does no title or property searches, which leaves that work to your title company. A name change on a recorded deed needs a new deed, and Ohio law allows only the requester or an attorney to draft it. The office has moved temporarily during construction at its building, so look up the service location on its website before visiting.

When a cash buyer makes sense

An as-is purchase makes sense when a firm closing date counts for more than a top price. Typical cases are a house with unfinished stormwater items, long-deferred upkeep, tenants in place, or a title that still needs sorting after an estate. The buyer takes on those problems, and the seller can often pick a closing day that fits a move.

Which county holds your Dublin parcel

Dublin sellers can list with an agent, go without one, or take a cash offer, but the first job is the same: find out which county records your parcel. The city spreads across Franklin, Delaware, Union and Madison counties, so deed transfer, valuation and recording follow whichever county holds your deed. Your tax bill or the county auditor's property search will tell you.

Dublin is a Columbus suburb of 49,094 people for July 2025, close to the 49,328 counted in 2020. It covers 24.44 square miles of land. Homes are pricey: the median owner-occupied value is $563,500 and 77.1 percent of the 17,995 households own. Median gross rent is $1,686, and owner costs with a mortgage run $3,055 a month against $1,349 without one. Median household income is $160,296.

Growth and the Bridge Street District

Dublin had 681 residents in 1970 and 3,855 in 1980, then 16,366 in 1990, as Interstate 270 and corporate headquarters arrived. It became a city in August 1987 after passing 5,000 people. The count reached 31,392 in 2000 and 49,328 in 2020, so most houses here are fairly recent construction.

Since 2020 the city has been redeveloping the Bridge Street District, 1,100 acres along the Scioto River with apartments, condominiums, retail and offices, including about 400 apartments and condominiums. Interstate 270 and State Route 161 are the main expressways, and the city is home to company headquarters that draw relocating buyers. If you sell near the district, expect questions about construction and future neighbors.

School districts

The Dublin City School District serves the city, and the Hilliard City School District serves a portion of it. Hilliard runs Washington Elementary School inside Dublin's limits. Dublin City has three high schools (Coffman, Scioto and Jerome), five middle schools and fifteen elementary schools.

The attendance boundary for the parcel, not the city name, decides the school. Confirm it before a listing names one.

Permits for work done before a sale

Dublin takes residential permit applications online through its Accela Citizen Access portal and an electronic plan review system. Residential means property with one, two or three family dwelling units. Projects that need permits include:

  • New homes and additions.
  • Interior remodeling, including basement remodels.
  • Decks and porches.
  • Swimming pools and hot tubs.

Fees are paid and the permit issued before work starts, and electrical, HVAC and plumbing contractors must be registered where registration is required. Ohio adds a 1 percent surcharge to residential fees other than plumbing and sewer or water fees. If a past remodel in your house skipped the permit, ask the city's Building Standards office what it takes to close it out before a buyer's inspection.

Code enforcement and deed restrictions

Dublin enforces zoning, health, parking, nuisance and sign codes. Most violation notices allow ten days to comply, and staff can allow more time in unusual circumstances. Every complaint is investigated first, and nothing follows if no violation turns up. Code Enforcement answers at 614.410.4600.

Zoning and private deed restrictions are separate matters. The city doesn't generally have standing to enforce a deed restriction. In many subdivisions an association does the enforcing, so gather the governing documents and confirm no dues are unpaid before you list. Buyers ask for both.

Short-term rentals before a sale

For the Delaware County part of Dublin, the Recorder charges $39 for the first two pages of a deed, which includes a $5 preservation surcharge, and $8 for each added page. Parcels in Franklin or Union County follow those counties' offices. Call the county auditor and recorder for current figures before you budget closing costs.

Ohio's disclosure rule

R.C. 5302.30 requires the owner of a home with one to four units to complete the state disclosure form for the buyer. If the buyer receives it late, after signing a contract, the buyer may cancel in writing for three business days from receipt. That right closes at the earlier of thirty days from acceptance or the closing date.

Give the form to buyers at the start of the listing so the cancellation clock never comes into play. Answer each item on it honestly and attach documents where you have them, such as repair invoices or permit records. A form filled in from memory invites follow-up questions, and a vague answer tends to cost more at the negotiating table than a plain one.

Paperwork buyers ask for

Build a folder before the first showing. Put in the signed state disclosure form, permits and final inspection records for any remodel, receipts for roof or HVAC work, and the association documents if your subdivision has one. Add the latest tax bill, which also shows the county that records your deed.

Buyers in a high-priced market read the paper trail closely. A clean folder answers most questions before they turn into price reductions, and it keeps an inspection report from becoming a negotiation over things you could have documented.

What to expect from contract to closing

Once you accept an offer, the title company confirms which county holds the deed, orders the property search and prepares the conveyance fee statement. Any open permit, unpaid association dues or recorded lien shows up in that search, so deal with those items early. Bring photo identification and any payoff letters to the signing.

A cash buyer removes the lender's appraisal and underwriting, which often makes the schedule shorter. The disclosure form, title search and recording still apply. Ask each buyer to put the price, the closing date and who pays each cost in writing, and compare offers on net proceeds rather than headline price.

Which county do I deal with when I sell a house in Dublin?

It depends on the parcel. Dublin falls within Franklin, Delaware, Union and Madison counties, so check your tax bill or the county auditor's property search to see which office records your deed.

Can I list my Dublin house on Airbnb to cover the mortgage while it sells?

Only with a city registration and within tight limits. Two weeks per calendar year is allowed, annual registration costs $225, and operating without registering carries a $250 fine.

How long do I have to fix a Dublin code violation?

Most notices give ten days, and code enforcement staff can extend that time when circumstances are unusual. Call Code Enforcement at 614.410.4600.

Does the city enforce my neighborhood's deed restrictions?

Generally not. The city lacks standing to pursue deed restrictions, so those fall to an association or neighbors. City zoning rules are separate.

What is Dublin's median home value?

The median value of an owner-occupied home is $563,500, and the owner-occupied rate is 77.1 percent.

What changes when a Lakewood owner sells a rental or a worn house?

Lakewood adds a city step for landlords: an owner who sells a non-owner-occupied rental needs a certificate of code compliance, which depends on a point of sale inspection. The certificate rule applies to non-owner occupied rentals only. For an owner living in the house, the choice runs among an agent, a by owner sale and a cash buyer.

  • Agent listing: reaches the most buyers for a tidy, updated house, with weeks set aside for inspections and financing.
  • Sale by owner: you set the price, run tours and complete the disclosure paperwork.
  • Cash buyer: takes the house in whatever shape it is in, which suits a double with deferred repairs, a rental with a pending inspection, or a house left by an estate.

Because only 44.4 percent of Lakewood homes are owner occupied, buyers and sellers here see rentals, doubles and small apartment buildings often. Knowing the city's rental rules early keeps a closing date from sliding.

Lakewood housing numbers

Lakewood had 49,027 residents on July 1, 2025, a 3.7 percent decline from the 2020 base of 50,930. It packs about 9,190 people into each of its 5.54 square miles of land, which explains the small lots and close neighbors a buyer will see on every block.

Older houses and neighborhoods

Lakewood grew as one of Cleveland's streetcar suburbs. Streetcars reached it on Detroit Avenue in 1893, Clifton Boulevard in 1903 and Madison Avenue in 1916, and the population jumped from 3,355 in 1900 to 70,509 by 1930. That history gave it the nickname City of Homes, and most of the housing stock is old.

Neighborhoods carry distinct building stock. Birdtown, an eight street district on the southeast side with bird names, was built in the 1890s for National Carbon Company workers and joined the National Register in 2006. Clifton Park in the northwest corner holds Victorian mansions near the lake, and Victorian Village on the east end housed company executives. Rockport Square added roughly 200 condos and lofts from 2004 along Detroit Avenue, and the Gold Coast high rises sit on the lakefront.

Schools, roads and the lakefront

Public schools belong to the Lakewood City School District, which includes Lakewood High School. Interstate 90 runs along the south side with ramps at West 117th Street, Bunts Road, Warren Road and McKinley Road. Greater Cleveland RTA buses cover Clifton Boulevard, Detroit Avenue, Madison Avenue, Warren Road and West 117th Street, and Red Line rapid stations sit just across the Cleveland border.

Lakewood Park is one of the largest lakefront parks in Ohio, and the Rocky River Reservation of the Cleveland Metroparks forms part of the western edge. Downtown Cleveland is about 6 miles to the east. Buyers who commute downtown will care about the bus and rail access, so mention it in a listing.

Housing licenses and point of sale inspection

Lakewood requires a housing license for any dwelling unit rented to another person, and the Housing and Building Department collects the fees. They run $75.00 per unit for non-owner occupied one or two family structures, $60.00 per unit for three family dwellings, $45.00 per unit for other non-owner occupied dwellings, and $200.00 per building for a vacant property license. Applications are due each November 1, and a late one adds $25.00 per unit.

Since September 1, 2019, a certificate of code compliance has been required before the sale of any non-owner occupied residential rental property. The point of sale inspection covers the interior, exterior and yard before the certificate issues, and the rules sit in Lakewood Codified Ordinances sections 1173.01 and 1306.53. To schedule one, call the Division of Housing and Building at (216) 529-6270 or write to building.permits@lakewoodoh.gov.

Start this process before you sign a purchase contract. An inspector's list of repairs is far easier to handle when you know about it at the start of a sale than at the closing table.

Deeds and rental registration in Cuyahoga County

Lakewood is in Cuyahoga County, where the Fiscal Officer's Real Estate Services office handles transfers and recording at 2079 E. Ninth Street, fourth floor, Cleveland. Recording closes at 4:00 p.m., so plan to arrive early. Each transfer needs a DTE 100 statement of value or a DTE 100 EX exemption statement. The standard recording charge is $39 for the opening pair of pages plus $8 per added page. For the conveyance fee rate that applies in Cuyahoga County, ask the Fiscal Officer before closing.

A separate county duty falls on rental owners. Ohio Revised Code 5323.02 requires a one time filing with the Fiscal Officer, with no fee, and any change must be reported within 60 days. A $50 penalty can follow each tax bill when the filing is missing, and the filing is needed even if the city has the rental on record. A buyer of your rental will need to file, and under Revised Code 319.202 the auditor's endorsement on the conveyance flags this.

Ohio's disclosure form

Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 requires the property disclosure form on one to four unit residential sales, with exceptions for fiduciary transfers and sales to a buyer who occupied the property for twelve months. Calling the sale as is does not replace the form, so a Lakewood double sold in poor shape still needs it, filled out with what you know.

Selling a Lakewood rental, step by step

Landlords should work through the city's requirements in order.

  1. Confirm the housing license is current and paid, since late fees add $25.00 per unit after November 1.
  2. Call (216) 529-6270 to schedule the point of sale inspection before you sign a contract.
  3. Fix what the inspector lists, then obtain the certificate of code compliance.
  4. Complete the disclosure form and a DTE 100 or DTE 100 EX statement for the county.
  5. Tell the buyer to file the rental registration with the Cuyahoga County Fiscal Officer under R.C. 5323.02.
  6. Have the title company record the deed before the 4:00 p.m. cutoff.

A cash buyer will often take on an inspection list and a lease as they stand, which saves an owner from running repairs while carrying a vacant unit.

Does a Lakewood rental need an inspection before it can be sold?

Yes. Lakewood's code requires a certificate of code compliance before the sale of a non-owner occupied residential rental, and a point of sale inspection comes first. Call (216) 529-6270 to schedule it.

What does a Lakewood housing license cost?

It costs $75.00 per unit for non-owner occupied one or two family structures, $60.00 per unit for three family dwellings, and $45.00 per unit for other non-owner occupied dwellings. Late applications after November 1 add $25.00 per unit.

Where do deeds for Lakewood houses get filed?

They go to the Cuyahoga County Fiscal Officer's Transfer and Recording office in Cleveland. A DTE 100 or DTE 100 EX form has to accompany the deed.

Is the disclosure form still required when a Lakewood house sells as is?

Usually yes. Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 covers sales of homes with up to four dwelling units, and calling the sale as is does not replace the form. Estate fiduciaries and several other transfers are exempt.

Does the buyer of my Lakewood rental have to register it with the county?

Yes, a new owner of residential rental property files with the Cuyahoga County Fiscal Officer under Revised Code 5323.02, even when the rental is already registered with the city. There is no filing fee, but a $50 penalty can follow each tax bill if the filing is missing.

Selling in Beavercreek

Greene County's largest city, Beavercreek, lies roughly five miles east of downtown Dayton, which puts many of its houses within an easy commute of Dayton employers. The 2025 population estimate is 48,134, about 3% above the 2020 count of 46,549.

Owners live in most of the homes here. The median home value is $279,600 and the median rent is $1,457. The city has 19,453 households averaging 2.39 people, and typical monthly owner costs run $1,837 with a mortgage and $838 without. Renters fill a bit more than a quarter of occupied homes, so investors and tenants round out the buyer pool.

Beavercreek incorporated as a city in February 1980 from part of the township, taking in the old settlements of Alpha, Knollwood, most of New Germany and Zimmerman. An older deed may still carry one of those place names. What a title company checks is the legal description and parcel number, never the neighborhood nickname.

With a long repair list, you can ask a direct buyer for an as-is offer and skip the renovation. Cash also avoids waiting on a lender's appraiser and the string of repair demands that tends to follow an inspection.

Permits and registrations that come up at sale

Permits split between the city and the county. The city's Planning and Development Department issues zoning permits, and Greene County Building Regulation handles building, plumbing, electrical and HVAC permits. Match each past project to its permit now, and you will find open work before a buyer's inspector does.

Permit Beavercreek requires for common residential projects
ProjectPermit or office
New house, addition or attached garageResidential Zoning Permit
DeckResidential Zoning Permit
Swimming poolSwimming Pool Permit
Shed or detached garage, propane tankAccessory Structure Permit

Interior remodel such as wall removal or a finished basementGreene County Building Regulation, no zoning permit

Zoning permits are not required for interior remodeling, at-grade patios, garage sales or driveways. You can apply in the online permit center or hand a printed form to staff at City Hall on Research Park Drive. If the house is vacant, ask the planning office whether the registration rule applies to it.

  • Greene County Building Regulation, at 667 Dayton-Xenia Road in Xenia, issues building, plumbing, electrical and HVAC permits.
  • Greene County Public Health, at 360 Wilson Drive in Xenia, is the contact for health department questions.
  • Greene County Sanitary Engineering, at the Dayton-Xenia Road address, handles sewer questions.
  • The Beavercreek Fire Department is at 851 N. Orchard Lane.

Renting your house by the night

Short-term rentals are allowed with a city license. Ordinance 23-15 and Chapter 117 of the city code require every owner to apply through the Online Permit Center before renting for fewer than thirty consecutive days. A license lasts two years and has to be renewed.

  • The application lists the location, where the unit will be advertised, bedrooms, maximum occupants, parking and emergency contacts.
  • Renters must be at least 25 years old, and owners must hand them house rules, noise rules and emergency details.
  • The city's 3% hotel, motel and short-term rental tax is filed quarterly, even for quarters with no rentals.

If an HOA governs your street, read its covenants before you advertise. If your house has run as a rental, tell buyers about the license and the tax filings, and ask the planning office whether a new owner must file a fresh application.

How Greene County processes a deed

Transfer of the deed runs through the Greene County Auditor, and the recorder files it once the auditor signs off. The auditor requires a completed Real Property Conveyance Statement of Value and Receipt (form DTE 100), and the grantor's name must match how the grantor took title in the previous deed. The county map department approves the deed before it reaches the auditor, and land in the farmland tax program needs the DTE 101 statement.

Expect two charges: fifty cents per parcel in transfer tax, plus a conveyance fee of $2 for every thousand dollars of sale price, rounded up to the nearest $100. The county runs an online calculator so you can see the amount for your sale.

The recorder also wants a complete legal description with the parcel number, a prepared-by statement, the prior deed reference and a notarial acknowledgment. A title company normally assembles all of this at closing, but it is worth confirming your name is spelled the same way on every document.

Property taxes and your closing

Each parcel gets a fair market value appraisal from the county auditor every six years, with an update in between at the three year mark. The auditor's office is at 69 Greene Street in Xenia, and staff appraisers can talk through a valuation or help you start an appeal. The money goes to schools, public safety, roads, libraries and parks.

Due dates are not fixed from year to year. House Bill 186's inflation cap credit, for example, once pushed back second-half bills in Greene County. For the year you close, get the schedule from the treasurer and let the title company prorate the tax so each side pays for the months they own the house.

Any taxes still owed come out of your proceeds at closing, so request a payoff figure early. Carry your latest tax bill, a copy of your deed, and a recent mortgage statement into your first call with the title company.

Schools, parks and transit

The Beavercreek City School District runs one preschool, six elementary schools, two middle schools, a Freshman School and Beavercreek High School. Beavercreek's parks department looks after 24 parks and properties, and Beavercreek Station is a hub on Creekside Trail, which runs from Xenia to Eastwood MetroPark in Dayton. The Greater Dayton Regional Transit Authority runs bus service in the city.

Buyers like these amenities. If you sell as is, ask the buyer to state in writing that repairs are theirs, and keep a copy of any inspection report you ordered. A sensible order of operations is permits first, deed paperwork second, a tax proration estimate third, and only then a side by side look at what each offer nets you. A cash buyer can usually pick a closing date that fits your move, which helps if you are relocating for work in the Dayton area. At the table you sign the deed in front of a notary, hand over the keys, and the title company sends your proceeds once the transfer goes through. If any permit sits unfinished, finishing it first usually costs less than a price cut later.

No permit is needed to sell. Check for open permits on past work, though, since decks, pools, fences and sheds need zoning permits and the county handles building, plumbing, electrical and HVAC permits.

What fees does Greene County charge on a deed?

A transfer tax of fifty cents per parcel and a conveyance fee of $2 per thousand dollars of the sale price, rounded up to the nearest $100. The county's online calculator shows the amount for your sale.

Can a Beavercreek short-term rental license pass to a buyer?

Ask the planning office. Licenses last two years and go to the owner who applies, so a new owner may need to file a new application through the Online Permit Center.

When are Greene County taxes due?

Dates are set each year and can move after state changes such as House Bill 186. Ask the Greene County Treasurer for the schedule that matches your closing.

Complete the Ohio property disclosure form if the home has up to four units. ORC 5302.30 lists exceptions such as estate sales and transfers to relatives, and the signed deed must be acknowledged before a notary under ORC 5301.01.

Before you agree to sell: Point of Sale

In Euclid, the order of operations is fixed by law. Before signing a sale agreement, the owner obtains a Point of Sale application and a Certificate of Code Compliance from the Housing Department, and the buyer receives the certificate. Chapter 1759 of the city's codified ordinances makes it unlawful to agree to sell or convey a dwelling without one in hand.

After you buy the application, a city inspector goes through the house and the lot. The resulting list of known violations drives your next move: repair the items, or let the buyer take them on. Start this step before you list, since the paperwork shapes both your price and your timeline.

Point of Sale fees and deadlines

Chapter 1759 spells out the terms in plain numbers, and every seller gets the same ones.

Euclid Point of Sale rules, Codified Ordinances Chapter 1759
SituationRule
Application fee$225.00, plus $35.00 per unit for buildings with more than three units

Owners of one or two family homes who sell and relocate within Euclid can apply for a rebate of the $225.00 fee when they buy another one or two family residence as their primary home. Assumed violations still open after 180 days can lead to prosecution under Section 1703.99.

Building and Housing office contacts

The Building, Housing and Nuisance Department takes calls Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., at (216) 289-2700. Extension 3908 covers Point of Sale and assumptions, 3904 residential permits, 3905 rental requirements, 3906 tall grass and yard debris, and 3903 vacant property registration. Send permit applications as email attachments to buildingandhousing@cityofeuclid.gov, because the office can't accept photos of forms.

  • Ask about the Point of Sale inspection before you list so the violation list is in your hands when buyers call.
  • Ask whether a vacant house must be registered with the city. Chapter 1763 ties exemptions to a current Point of Sale inspection and a for sale status.
  • Fence and shed questions go to the same office. The city caps combined garage and shed area at 696 square feet and allows no shed taller than ten feet.

The city's Housing Accessibility and Rehabilitation Grant Program excludes problems found in a Point of Sale inspection, so don't plan on it to pay for sale repairs.

Owning in Euclid: what buyers weigh

Euclid is an inner ring Cleveland suburb on Lake Erie, in Cuyahoga County. Population is 47,962 for July 2025, down 3.5 percent from the April 2020 base. Owners live in 46.4 percent of homes, so rentals are a large part of the market.

  • Median gross rent: $1,025
  • Households: 22,433, averaging 2.16 people
  • Median household income: $50,285

The city sits in the Lake Erie Snowbelt, so lake squalls test roofs, gutters and driveways every winter, and buyers inspect those items closely. Euclid City Schools is the public district. A rental owner who sells should know that Ohio Revised Code 5323.02 requires owners of residential rental property to file ownership details with the county Fiscal Officer.

Recording the deed in Cuyahoga County

The Cuyahoga County Fiscal Office Transfer and Recording division, at 2079 E. Ninth Street, 4th floor, Cleveland, phone 216-443-2060, handles the deed. Every transfer needs either a DTE 100 Statement of Value and Receipt or a DTE 100-EX exemption form. Office hours are Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., with recording until 4:00 p.m.

Recording costs $39 for the first two pages and $8 for each page after. Preparing a deed counts as the practice of law, and county staff can't advise on it, so a title company or attorney normally drafts it.

The state form and the city form

Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 asks sellers of one to four unit homes to deliver a signed property disclosure form to buyers. A Euclid seller usually completes both that state form and the city's Point of Sale paperwork.

They do different jobs. The city's certificate reports code violations found by an inspector. The state form is your own statement about the condition of the house. Neither replaces the other, and buyers will read them side by side.

Selling a Euclid house with violations

Open violations don't kill a sale. They change who does the work. With the Assumption application, the buyer agrees to correct the listed items within 180 days of transfer, and those items stay open until then. A buyer who plans to renovate anyway may welcome that arrangement, and it lets you skip repairs you wouldn't have recovered in the price.

Repairing first suits a seller who wants a wider pool of buyers, especially buyers using a lender, who may balk at a long violation list. Compare the cost of the repairs with the discount a buyer asks for. If a certificate lapses after six months with no sale, you can renew it for 50% of the original fee by reporting in writing within 30 days of expiration.

A step by step plan for a Euclid sale

First, call extension 3908 and buy the Point of Sale application. Second, let the inspector visit and read the violation list carefully. Third, decide which items you will repair and which the buyer will assume, keeping the 180-day correction window in mind. Fourth, complete the state disclosure form and gather repair receipts.

Once you have a contract, hand the certificate to the buyer and have the deed prepared by a title company or attorney. The deed goes to the Cuyahoga County Fiscal Office with a DTE 100 or DTE 100-EX form, and recording follows. If the property sold within the six months of the certificate, no new inspection is needed.

A cash buyer will often accept the house with violations, which removes the repair step, though the Assumption application and the 180-day correction window still apply to that buyer. Ask each buyer for a written price, closing date and cost split, and compare offers side by side.

Frequently asked questions

Does Euclid require an inspection before I sell?

Yes. Chapter 1759 requires a Point of Sale application and a Certificate of Code Compliance before you agree to sell, and the buyer must receive a copy. The application fee is $225.00.

What if my Euclid house fails the Point of Sale inspection?

You can fix the violations, or the buyer can take them on by filing an Assumption application and correcting them within 180 days of the transfer. Call extension 3908 at (216) 289-2700 for the steps.

How long does a Euclid Certificate of Code Compliance last?

Six months. If the property sells during that period, no new Point of Sale inspection is required for the sale.

Can a senior pay less for the Euclid Point of Sale application?

Yes. The fee falls to $100.00 for elderly Euclid homeowners who receive the Cuyahoga County homestead exemption, except when the property transfers because the owner died.

Where is a Euclid deed filed?

With the Cuyahoga County Fiscal Office Transfer and Recording division in Cleveland, along with a DTE 100 or DTE 100-EX form. Call 216-443-2060 to confirm what your document needs.

Ways to sell a Mansfield house

In Mansfield you can list with a broker, line up your own purchaser, or accept an as-is offer from an investor paying cash. Three things tend to decide it: what repairs would cost, whether a move or court date is forcing the timing, and who lives in the house now.

Many houses here are older, so furnaces, wiring and roofs come up often. Financed buyers inspect and negotiate, while cash buyers set their own terms. However you sell, the deed finishes by going through three county desks: tax map, auditor and recorder.

  • Listing with a broker suits a tidy house and a seller who can wait a few months.
  • A private sale suits a relative, tenant or neighbor already interested.
  • Cash suits an estate, a worn-out rental or a short fuse.

Mansfield housing numbers

Mansfield has 47,381 residents and owners live in 50.5 percent of its homes. About 19.9 percent of residents are 65 or older, which tends to mean steady demand for smaller, easy-to-maintain houses. Population is nearly flat, down 0.2 percent from the 2020 base.

Mansfield measureFigure
Population estimate, July 202547,381
Households, 2020-202419,516
People per household2.13
Median owner-occupied home value$119,600
Median gross rent$814

Location and the local economy

Mansfield sits about halfway between Cleveland and Columbus along Interstate 71, in hilly country west of the Allegheny Plateau. Interstate 71 reaches the city through three exits. The Martin Luther King Jr. Freeway, which is U.S. 30, is the one limited-access road inside the city and heads toward Bucyrus in the west and Wooster in the east.

The city once made tires, stoves, brass goods and appliances, and most of that work is gone. Employers that remain include Therm-O-Disc, The Gorman-Rupp Company, Ideal Electric and The Carousel Works, along with a service sector built on health care and education. The city calls itself the Carousel Capital of Ohio.

Buyers can choose among Ohio State University at Mansfield, North Central State College and an Ashland University nursing building on Trimble Road, all nearby.

Schools and your address

Mansfield City Schools operate eight schools, including a Spanish immersion school, and the Madison Local School District covers the eastern parts of the city. Because two districts reach into the city, confirm the right one for your address before it goes in a listing. The county auditor's parcel record or a call to the district will settle it.

Also decide early what you will do with belongings. A house sold as is can be emptied or left with its contents, and saying so in the first conversation with a buyer saves a round of renegotiating near closing. Take photos of anything you plan to leave, and note any item that conveys with the house.

Winters and an older house

Snowfall averages 49.2 inches a season and the mean January temperature is 26.5 degrees Fahrenheit. A December 2004 ice storm brought a record 23 inches of snow in 24 hours. Local buyers know that history and often ask how old the roof is and what shape the insulation, sump pump and furnace are in. Receipts for past work answer those questions fast, so keep them where you can find them.

How a deed moves through Richland County

Richland County accepts electronic deed transfers, and each deed must include tax map pre-approval. Anything needing tax map or auditor review must be carried to the courthouse by hand.

Both the recorder and the auditor are at 50 Park Avenue East. Recording of documents ends at 3:45 p.m. Do not expect forms or legal guidance there; the recorder points people to an attorney.

  • Request tax map pre-approval first.
  • Hand-deliver anything the auditor must review.
  • Let a title company or lawyer handle the legal description.

Starting with the tax map step avoids the most common delay, a deed that is turned away at the window because the approval is missing.
