Selling a house in Warren

Warren is the Trumbull County seat, on the Mahoning River about 14 miles northwest of Youngstown and 56 miles southeast of Cleveland. Selling here means dealing with a city whose rules for rentals, vacant houses and contractors are written into its Codified Ordinances. The population is an estimated 38,328, below the 39,201 counted in 2020 and the 41,557 counted in 2010.

The steps below cover the city and county offices a seller meets, starting with the numbers.

Housing costs and condition

The city has low values and many renters.

  • Owners occupy 56.1% of housing units.
  • The middle owner-occupied house is valued at $86,400.
  • Owners pay $967 a month with a mortgage and $409 without one.
  • Gross rent at the midpoint is $766.
  • There are 16,871 households with 2.16 people each.
  • Household income at the midpoint is $37,887.

At these values a repair bill can equal a large share of the price. Buyers weigh condition closely and expect the seller to say what's wrong. Many older buildings from the late 19th and early 20th centuries still stand around Courthouse Square, and the mills that built the town are long gone, so expect aged systems in a lot of houses.

Rental dwelling permits

Under section 1367.10 of Warren's Codified Ordinances, no dwelling unit without at least one owner living in it can be occupied without a residential non-owner occupied dwelling permit from the Health Officer's office. The permit is issued after a Building Inspector confirms compliance with the Housing, Building, Zoning and fire codes.

  • The annual fee for a single-unit dwelling is $120, and multi-unit buildings pay $100 per unit for two to fifty units, with lower per-unit rates above that.
  • A permit lasts one year and can't be transferred to a new owner, so whoever buys a tenant-occupied house applies in their own name.
  • The Water Department won't open service for a non-owner-occupied unit without proof of the permit.
  • Occupying a unit without a permit carries a $1,000 fine, and each day counts as a separate violation.

Before listing a rental, ask the Health Department whether the permit is current, and tell the buyer it doesn't travel with the deed.

When an empty house counts as vacant

Chapter 1338 sets up a Vacant Property Registry. An owner has 30 days after a structure becomes vacant to register it with the Code Official. The annual fee is $200 for a residential structure, though it can be avoided if the property is secured, free of trash, mowed, and shows a visible address. Missing the filing deadline costs $50 per day up to $1,000.

One rule bears directly on a sale. A house under a signed broker listing agreement isn't counted as vacant during the first six months of that listing, while an empty house offered for sale by its owner counts as vacant immediately. If you've moved out and plan to sell without a broker, register or secure the property first.

Hiring a contractor before you sell

You don't always need one. Chapter 1305 makes contractors register with the city, posting a $25,000 surety bond and showing insurance, yet it exempts a homeowner working on the single-family house they live in. That owner files a waiver of liability with the Building Division, and permits under Chapter 1307 still apply.

A hired contractor must hold the registration first, and one who starts without it pays double the fee. Ask any contractor for the city registration before work begins.

How the Trumbull County Board of Revision works

Three county offices, the Auditor, the Treasurer and the Commissioners, or their representatives, make up the board. It rules on value complaints and on denied homestead or owner-occupancy claims, and it leaves the tax dollars on your bill alone. Whoever files carries the burden of proof.

  • Complaints go to the Auditor's office, which acts as the board's secretary. Email goes to BOR@co.trumbull.oh.us. A handwritten form needs a notary, and a typed form sent by email does not.
  • Useful evidence includes appraisals, photos, repair estimates and a recent settlement statement and purchase agreement.
  • Notice of a hearing arrives at least ten days ahead, and you may attend in person, by phone or on video.

The filing window under Ohio Revised Code 5715.19 closes at the end of March following the tax year. An outside party can seek a higher value only when a recent arm's length sale beat the listed value by ten percent and by a state threshold, set at $567,000 for tax year 2025.

Schools and downtown

The Warren City School District runs four preK to 8 schools and Warren G. Harding High School. Declining population led to a redistricting plan, a new Harding building and the demolition of several early 20th century elementary and junior high schools, so a buyer comparing school buildings should ask the district which one serves a given street.

Downtown still centers on the Trumbull County Courthouse, built beginning in 1895, along with a Carnegie Law Library and bank and office buildings from the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

Selling an inherited house

Many Warren sales start with an estate. Under Ohio Revised Code 5302.30, an heir who hasn't lived in the house during the past year is excused from the state disclosure form, and so is a fiduciary selling for an estate, guardianship or trust. Other sellers of one-to-four unit homes must hand over the signed form.

Even then, buyers ask about known defects, so answer in writing and keep a copy.

Roads and winter showings

A freeway carrying Ohio 82 bypasses the city, and Ohio 5 leads southwest to the Ohio Turnpike. US 422 and Ohio 45 also run through Warren. The city sees about 27.9 inches of snow per year on 21 snowy days, and January lows average 16.8 degrees. Plan showings around plowed walks, working heat and visible roof and gutter condition, since buyers check these first in winter.

A short checklist before you list

Warren sellers can save time by sorting the city items first. If the house is a rental, confirm the dwelling permit and tell the buyer it won't transfer. If you've moved out and plan to sell without a broker, register the vacant property or secure it so the fee can be avoided. If you plan repairs, check whether the contractor is registered, or file the owner waiver if you're doing the work yourself.

Then turn to the county. Decide whether the value complaint window is still open, and whether any homestead or owner-occupancy claim needs attention before closing. A cash buyer who takes the house as-is won't ask for a repair list, but the permit, registry and disclosure rules still apply to the sale, so it pays to have them straight before the first offer arrives.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a permit to sell a rental house in Warren?

The dwelling permit in section 1367.10 does not transfer when the house sells. The buyer applies for a new one, and the Water Department wants proof of it before opening service.

What if I move out and list the house myself?

An empty house offered for sale by its owner counts as vacant under Chapter 1338 and must be registered within 30 days. A broker-listed house gets a six-month pass from the start of the listing.

When is the deadline to dispute my property value in Trumbull County?

By the end of March after the tax year, or the first-half collection date when that is later. Call the Auditor at 330-675-2420 for the current dates.

Does an inherited house need the Ohio disclosure form?

Usually not. Section 5302.30 excuses an heir who hasn't lived in the house for a year and also excuses fiduciaries acting for an estate.

Can I keep my homestead exemption after I sell?

No. The exemption belongs to the home you own and live in on January 1, so it ends with the sale. Your next home needs its own application with the county auditor.

Before you sell in Westerville

Westerville is a northeast suburb of Columbus that straddles two counties, Franklin and Delaware. That split decides which auditor, which board of revision and which health district you deal with. Population is about 38,165, down from 39,190 in 2020. The city runs its own electric and water utilities and collects no property tax at all.

The sections below start with where your parcel sits, then go through city steps, county filings and state paperwork for a sale.

Westerville homeownership figures

For 2020 to 2024 the picture is a mid-priced suburb with a settled owner base.

  • Owner-occupied housing rate: 72.5%.

Interstates 71 and 270 border the city, State Route 3 runs through Uptown as State Street, and central Westerville is about 16 miles from downtown Columbus and 12 miles from John Glenn Columbus International Airport by interstate. Otterbein University and the Uptown district anchor the older part of town.

Which county handles your house?

The city sits across the Franklin and Delaware county line, so start with the auditor's parcel search to see which county bills your house. The Franklin County Auditor's office is at 614-525-4663 and the Delaware County Auditor's office is at 740-833-2900.

Building Division permits

The Building Division is a state-certified department inside Planning and Development, reachable at 614-901-6650. It reviews plans before work starts and issues a Certificate of Occupancy or a Final Approval after inspections. Permit fees are paid when you pick up the permit, and plans go in through the city's Plan Review Portal.

  • Permits cover new buildings, alterations, signs, fences, pools, patio covers, decks, garages and satellite dishes, and fences carry no permit fee.
  • The city doesn't require a homeowner or contractor to hold a city license before pulling a permit.
  • A home occupation can need a conditional use permit.

Ask the division for your permit history before you list, and close out any permit that never received a final approval.

Utilities and trash at closing

Westerville supplies electric and water service itself, while sewer treatment comes through Columbus and refuse through Rumpke. All four charges appear on one bill that is due on the 15th of the month after it is issued. Utility Billing sits at 21 S. State Street and answers at 614-901-6430. Sewer charges follow water use.

  • Refuse and recycling go out every Tuesday, and yard waste goes out every Monday.

  • Owners must keep yards and vacant lots free of trash, debris, overgrown grass and weeds. Code Enforcement takes calls at 614-901-6650.
  • A garage sale needs no permit, but it is limited to one every six months and three consecutive days.

Schedule the final meter reading with Utility Billing as part of the closing checklist so the buyer's service starts clean.

Snow and storm rules

Winter showings run into city rules. Plows clear all city streets once snow passes two inches, and a snow emergency starts automatically above three inches, after which cars left on the street can be towed. Owners must keep the walkway in front of the house clear of snow and ice.

The city removes fallen limbs from street trees, but a tree or branch that comes down from private property is the owner's job to remove. Westerville also offers free residential fire inspections at 614-901-6600, a quick safety check before a buyer's inspector arrives.

Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 applies to sales of homes with one to four units. The seller completes the state disclosure form and delivers a signed copy to the buyer or the buyer's agent. Receiving it late opens a short rescission window, so hand it over before the offer is signed.

Value disputes follow ORC 5715.19. The complaint is due by March 31 of the next year, or the first-half collection closing date if that falls later.

Steps for a quick Westerville sale

Start by learning which county your parcel is in, because that sets the auditor you call, the board of revision you'd use and the health district that serves the house. Then pull the permit history from the Building Division and close out anything that never got a final approval. Open permits are one of the easiest things for a buyer's lender to catch late.

Next, get the yard and walkways in order, since Code Enforcement can act on overgrown grass, trash and debris. Book the final meter reading with Utility Billing for the closing date. Finally, complete the state disclosure form and hand it over before the offer is signed.

A cash buyer who accepts the house as-is can shorten the schedule, because there's no lender appraisal to wait on. Every one of the steps above still applies, though, and doing them early lets you accept a fast closing date without scrambling.

If you think the county value is too high, the timing matters as much as the evidence. Franklin County's filing season and Delaware County's window both close March 31, and Delaware accepts complaints starting January 2. Bring photos, repair estimates or a recent purchase agreement to the hearing, which usually runs 10 to 20 minutes. Remember that the board decides value only, so a complaint about the tax bill itself goes nowhere. Landlords selling a rental should confirm the registration with the auditor before closing, since the county tracks owner contact details and the buyer will need to update them.

Frequently asked questions

Does the City of Westerville collect property taxes?

No. County governments collect property taxes for every taxing district. Call the Franklin County Auditor at 614-525-4663 or the Delaware County Auditor at 740-833-2900, depending on where your parcel sits.

Do I need a permit to build a fence before I sell a Westerville house?

Yes, a permit is required to build, replace, relocate or alter a fence, though the city charges no permit fee. Call the Zoning Division at 614-901-6662.

Who collects trash at a Westerville house?

Refuse and recycling are collected Tuesdays and yard waste Mondays, and Rumpke provides refuse service. Containers go out no earlier than 6 p.m. the evening before and no later than 7 a.m. on collection day.

What is Westerville's income tax rate?

The city rate is 2.00%, and all adult residents and businesses file city returns. Ask the city's tax office at 614-901-6420 how a sale affects your filing.

How do I find out which county my Westerville house is in?

Search the parcel on either county auditor's website, or look at the property tax bill. Franklin and Delaware counties run separate boards of revision, health districts and auditor offices.

Fastest ways to sell a North Ridgeville house

You can hire a listing agent, sell on your own, or accept a cash purchase where the buyer takes the house with every flaw. Listing reaches the most buyers. A cash sale gives up some price in return for speed and no repair work. Lorain County, not the city, controls the deed paperwork, so the filing steps below follow the county auditor.

North Ridgeville housing at a glance

North Ridgeville is a growing suburb on the eastern edge of Lorain County, about 18 miles west of downtown Cleveland. It covers 23.58 square miles. Most addresses use ZIP code 44039, with some sections on 44035, 44011 and 44044. Census counts rose from 22,338 residents in 2000 to 29,465 in 2010 and 35,280 in 2020, and the mid-2025 estimate is 37,786.

Permits and zoning before you sell

The Building Division issues permits, registers contractors and enforces zoning and property maintenance codes. Plans that need review can take three weeks or more, and every permit comes with a list of required inspections, each of which must be booked at least a day ahead.

Residential projects are checked for zoning compliance when the permit application arrives. Additions, decks, swimming pools, accessory storage buildings and fences are the usual triggers. Walk the property before listing and make sure earlier work was permitted and closed out. A phone call to the Building Division will tell you if an open permit or code notice is attached to the address, which a buyer's title search can turn up.

How the deed transfer works in Lorain County

A North Ridgeville sale is finished at the Lorain County Auditor, which stamps the deed and collects the conveyance fee before the document is recorded. The Real Estate Department takes transfers in person or through an approved e-file vendor, Monday through Thursday only. E-filed transfers are cut off at 3 p.m., and walk-in transfers at 4 p.m.

Mail-in transfers ended on November 1, 2012. Handwritten forms are refused, and incomplete forms or wrong fees come back unprocessed. Staff cannot fill in forms or answer legal questions, so a closing agent or lawyer normally files for you.

Three Ohio statutes shape the paperwork. Section 5302.30 requires most owners of small residential buildings to give buyers a condition disclosure. Section 319.202 calls for a sworn statement of value and puts the conveyance fee on the seller. Section 322.02 lets a county add its own transfer tax, up to 30 cents for every hundred dollars of value, paid by the grantor before recording. The auditor's website has a conveyance fee calculator you can use to estimate the charge.

Property taxes when you sell

The Lorain County Treasurer bills North Ridgeville property in two halves, and the settlement sheet divides the amount owed between you and the buyer. Ohio bills run a year behind, so the bill that arrives in your sale year pays for the year before. The treasurer's office is in Room 201 of the Lorain County Administration Building in Elyria. Call it for the current due dates, since they can shift when the state changes a credit.

The treasurer also runs a monthly escrow plan for owners who prefer to spread the bill out.

Two county programs can matter to a seller. Owners who occupy the house as their residence on January 1 can apply for the 2.5 percent owner-occupancy reduction, which the auditor says is often arranged during the transfer. A valuation complaint to the county board of revision costs nothing and may be filed from the first of January through March 31, usually once per three-year cycle unless an exception such as an arm's length sale applies.

A cash buyer is worth a call when time or condition is what stands in your way: an inherited house no one wants to rehab, a rental emptying out, or a new job with a start date. The buyer takes the flaws, which removes repairs, staging and the lender's appraisal.

Compare the net you would see from a listing, not the headline number. Put the closing date in the contract, learn who pays the county conveyance fee and title charges, and ask if open permits are acceptable. Declining costs nothing, so collect an offer next to your agent's price opinion.

Gather the condition disclosure, permit records for past work, your latest tax bill and a note of anything the Building Division has flagged. Give your closing agent or lawyer the full set early, because the auditor returns incomplete forms and every rejection can delay closing.

Frequently asked questions

Which office handles the deed in a North Ridgeville sale?

The Lorain County Auditor's Real Estate Department, because the city lies in Lorain County. It takes walk-in and e-filed transfers Monday through Thursday, and your closing agent or lawyer usually submits the right conveyance form.

Must I give a condition disclosure to North Ridgeville buyers?

Usually, yes. Section 5302.30 of the Ohio code asks owners of homes with up to four units to deliver the completed form promptly, and a buyer handed it only after signing gets three business days to back out. Transfers by an estate fiduciary, and some inherited homes you never lived in, are exempt.

Can I challenge my valuation before I sell?

You can try, within limits. In Lorain County the complaint must be filed or postmarked by March 31 and carries no fee. It is normally allowed once per three-year period unless the property sold at arm's length, was substantially improved or suffered casualty damage.

Does North Ridgeville inspect a house before it sells?

The city's building and zoning pages cover permits for construction work, with no inspection tied to a sale. Ask the Building Division whether an open permit or code notice sits on your address, then close it out so the title search comes back clean.

How long does a cash sale in North Ridgeville take?

The contract decides. With no lender appraisal, the pace comes from title work and the closing date you negotiate. Spell out the date, the fee split and the as-is terms before you sign.

Selling a rental in Gahanna

A buyer who keeps the property as a rental must register it within 30 days of the transfer. Gahanna's Ordinance 0053-2018 requires every residential rental owner to register every two years.

  • Registration runs between January 1 and March 15, and approved permits expire December 31 of the second year.

Preparing a Gahanna house for a buyer

Buyers in a market with strong incomes expect a tidy inspection report. Before you list, walk the property for the items the city codes cover: exterior condition, yard debris, parking and any posted notice. Fix what you can and keep receipts. If a city notice is open, ask Code Enforcement how to close it out, because an unresolved report can slow a buyer's lender.

Gather the deed, the latest tax bill and the state disclosure form. Landlords should add the lease and the registration paperwork. If an owner has died, bring whatever proves who may sign. These are the first things a title company asks for, and having them ready keeps the days between contract and closing short.

Franklin County conveyance fee

The Franklin County Auditor bills $3 per $1,000 of price on a standard sale, split between a $1 state share and a $2 county share, and adds a $0.50 transfer tax. Use the Auditor's online calculator, which asks you to round the price up to the next $100 and applies a $3 floor.

The county share is waived when the seller holds the homestead exemption on the transfer date, which cuts the rate to $1 per $1,000. An exempt conveyance owes just the $0.50. The calculator accepts cash, business checks and cashier's checks payable to the Franklin County Auditor and turns away personal checks, and the amount must be exact.

ORC 319.202 puts the statement of value on the buyer's side and makes the seller pay the fee. Value includes any mortgage or lien. The Transfer and Conveyance department answers questions at 614-525-3253.

Homestead status before you sign

Check your homestead exemption before closing. The standard credit goes to owners aged 65 by year-end or permanently and totally disabled, within an income cap. Owners who are 100 percent disabled through military service can qualify for an enhanced credit with no income test.

The Auditor's Homestead office is at 373 S High St, 21st Floor, Columbus, or homestead@franklincountyohio.gov. Whether you hold the exemption on the closing date decides the conveyance rate. If you think you qualify but never applied, ask the office before you set a closing date, since the timing affects what you owe.

Commuting and downtown

Gahanna works as a commuter base, which helps a listing aimed at people who work elsewhere in the Columbus area. Interstate 670 and US 62 lead to John Glenn Columbus International Airport, Interstate 270 rings the area, Ohio 317 is the main north-south street through downtown, and COTA runs bus lines 24 and 25 through the center. The city uses ZIP code 43230 and sits on 12.43 square miles of land.

The Gahanna-Jefferson Public School District serves the city, and Gahanna-Lincoln is its high school. Downtown redevelopment has been part of the pitch since 2004. The Creekside project added a park extension, restaurants, offices, residences and a 389-space garage. Verify the district for your address with the county, because the Jefferson Township pockets can differ.

Creeks and drainage

Properties along Big Walnut Creek, Rocky Fork Creek and Sycamore Run deserve a flood and drainage check before listing. Ask the Franklin County Auditor's office or the city for the zone of your parcel, and keep any insurance, drainage or sump-pump records handy. Gahanna-Jefferson Public Schools, whose high school is Gahanna-Lincoln. Small Jefferson Township pockets sit within city limits, so verify the district for your address with the county.

The seller pays under ORC 319.202, and the buyer files the statement of value. Your purchase contract may restate or shift it, so read the closing section.

What to check first in Upper Arlington

Upper Arlington is a planned suburb on the northwest side of Columbus. A sale here turns on lot layout, school boundaries and a few city rules that older houses trigger. The city sits entirely in Franklin County, with the Scioto River along its west edge. The population is about 35,893, down from 36,800 in 2020. This page covers what the city inspects, what the county handles and what Ohio expects from a seller on paper, so you can judge how fast a sale can move.

Two housing stocks on one map

Two brothers who developed real estate bought the first 840 acres south of present-day Lane Avenue in 1913 and followed a Garden City plan with deep setbacks, parks and separate zones for shops and apartments. The village incorporated in 1918, and cityhood came on February 8, 1941. Annexations, mostly between the late 1940s and 1960, built out the rest. The result:

  • South of Lane Avenue, the Old Arlington district holds Colonial and English Revival houses. The district was added to the National Register in 1985.
  • North of Lane, post-war tracts such as River Ridge follow ordinary street grids with ranch houses, and houses built from the 1960s on grew larger.

Which side of Lane Avenue your house sits on decides which city rules you meet first.

What homeownership costs here

This is a pricey, owner-heavy suburb, so buyers compare your house against a high-priced local market. Condition and presentation carry weight.

  • About 79.4% of housing units are lived in by their owners.
  • The typical owner-occupied house is valued at $595,600.
  • Monthly ownership costs run $3,189 for households with a mortgage and $1,284 for those without.
  • The city holds 14,330 households averaging 2.52 people.
  • Household income at the midpoint is $155,167.
  • Roughly 88.2% of residents were in the same home twelve months earlier.

The Upper Arlington City School District serves the whole city, and its high school was rebuilt in 2021. Downtown Columbus and the Ohio State campus are a short drive away.

The Old Arlington demolition rule

It can matter if the buyer plans to tear the house down. In 2009 City Council adopted rules meant to discourage, without prohibiting, total demolition of historically significant homes. A six-month delay period gives owners and the city time to look for alternatives, and the rules appear in Articles 5, 6 and 7 of the Unified Development Ordinance.

The city's GIS maps show which properties are identified as historically significant, and Community Development posts a Guide to Demolition in the Historic District along with an owner statement and a demolition sign affidavit. Selling a house south of Lane Avenue to a builder or investor? Tell the buyer up front and ask Community Development whether your parcel is flagged.

City offices for permits and exterior complaints

Community Development runs three divisions: Planning, Building and Code Compliance. The office at 3600 Tremont Road keeps weekday hours of 8 am to 5 pm. The main line is 614-583-5070, and inspections are 614-583-5080.

Exterior upkeep is mostly complaint driven. High grass and weeds, flaking paint, illegal temporary signs, excess lighting, trash and debris, and noise are the common violations. A confirmed complaint brings a written Notice of Violation with a re-inspection date, which an officer may extend for substantial progress, bad weather or other mitigating circumstances. Most violations carry a maximum of $150 per offense per day, and a few are fourth degree misdemeanors with a $250 maximum fine and up to 30 days in jail.

Clearing out a cluttered or dated house

Bulk items go to the curb by 7 am on your regular collection day, and mattresses and box springs must be wrapped in plastic. Large appliances and anything containing Freon may cost extra, so ask Local Waste Services at 614-409-9375, option 2, before you set them out.

  • One garage or yard sale per residence is allowed in any six-month period, for no more than three consecutive days, with no permit.
  • A plumbing permit is needed to install or replace a boiler, water heater or water meter, or any time supply or waste lines change.
  • Decks, fences, driveway replacements, detached garages and pools each appear as their own permit type in the online system.

Finished basements, new decks and swapped water heaters are the usual places a permit gap shows up. Pull the permit history first and close any gap before you accept an offer.

Rental registration and value complaints

Because the whole city is in Franklin County, one auditor handles both topics. Landlords file owner or manager contact details with that office under Ohio Revised Code 5323.02, within 60 days of the notice that follows a property transfer or of receiving a tax bill. A property left unfiled draws a $150 fine for each tax year, and an owner living outside Ohio has to name an Ohio contact.

A value complaint also starts at the auditor. ORC 5715.19 sets the cutoff at the end of March after the tax year, or the day first-half collection closes if that is later. The Board of Revision looks at the property's value only, so the tax bill itself is outside its scope.

Franklin's standard Homestead Exemption helps lower-income owners who turn 65 by year-end or are permanently and totally disabled. An enhanced version for owners with a 100% service-connected disability rating shields $50,000 of appraised value from tax and has no income test.

What an Ohio seller must hand the buyer

Ohio's residential disclosure statute, section 5302.30, has the seller complete a state form about the condition of the property and pass a signed copy to the buyer early. If it arrives after the contract, the buyer gets a short window to back out, and that window also applies when the form never shows up.

Answer each item honestly and amend the form if facts change. Where you truly don't know an answer, the statute allows a good faith estimate.

Comparing ways to sell quickly

The trade is time against price. An agent listing puts the house in front of owner-occupant buyers, which means showings and waiting on a lender. A direct as-is purchase can shorten the wait, and the offer drops by whatever repairs the buyer absorbs.

  • Get each offer in writing with the closing date, who covers closing costs and which repairs are excluded.
  • Request proof of funds before you sign.
  • Look up the permit history and any open exterior complaint before listing, since both can push a closing date.

A buyer who pays cash and skips the lender removes the loan approval step, but the city and county tasks above stay on your list. Do them in this order: permit history, open complaints, disclosure form, then the offer.

Does Upper Arlington require a permit for a deck or fence?

Yes. Decks and fences each appear as residential permit types in the city's online system. Call Community Development at 614-583-5070 before work begins and confirm that earlier projects on your house were closed out.

Can a buyer tear down my Old Arlington house?

Often yes, after a delay. The 2009 rules in the Unified Development Ordinance set a six-month delay period for total demolition of historically significant homes. Ask Community Development whether your parcel is identified in the city's GIS maps.

Do I need to register a rental house in Upper Arlington before selling it?

The registration comes from the county auditor, not the city, and rests on Ohio Revised Code 5323.02. A missing filing carries a $150 fine per tax year, so update the contact record before closing. The auditor's line is 614-525-4663.

When can I dispute my home's value?

File with the Franklin County Auditor by the end of March after the tax year, or the first-half collection deadline when that is later. The Board of Revision, at 614-525-3913, rules on value only.

Who completes the Ohio property disclosure form?

The seller does. Section 5302.30 covers most sales of homes with up to four units, and some transfers, such as gifts to a spouse or a relative in the direct line, fall outside it.

Sellers in Mason generally choose between hiring a broker, handling the sale alone, or taking an as-is cash buyer. Once a contract exists, the county steps do not change, and each one goes through the Warren County auditor and recorder.

Speed is what you are trading. Listing the usual way can draw plenty of buyers along with inspection credits, staging work and weeks of showings. Selling straight for cash avoids most of that, and the closing date is yours to pick.

Mason home values

Mason's median owner-occupied home is valued at $426,200 for 2020-2024, and owners live in 80.1 percent of the housing. The July 1, 2025 estimate is 35,834 people, 3.0 percent over the 2020 base.

Median household income is $125,401 and median gross rent is $1,760. The city counts 13,502 households of 2.60 people on average. With values at this level, even a modest repair list can shift an offer noticeably, so collect a few contractor quotes before deciding how much to fix.

Annual precipitation runs 44.68 inches, with July highs near 87 degrees and January lows near 19, so roofs and gutters work through a full range of seasons.

Mason's setting and employers

Mason lies about 22 miles north of downtown Cincinnati and covers roughly 19 square miles. Corporate employers anchor the local economy. Cintas is headquartered here, along with the Procter & Gamble Mason Business Center and the headquarters of Luxottica Retail, and more than 90 companies run headquarters or manufacturing sites across the city's 24 commerce parks.

Kings Island amusement park and the Lindner Family Tennis Center, home of the Cincinnati Open, also sit in Mason. Workers at these employers make up a steady share of local buyers, and many of them want a move-in-ready house, so describe the condition honestly.

  • Seven city parks cover about 300 acres, with lakes, trails and ball fields.

Schools

Mason City Schools serves the city with five public schools: Mason Early Childhood Center for pre-K through second grade, Mason Elementary for grades 3 and 4, Mason Intermediate for grades 5 and 6, Mason Middle for grades 7 and 8, and William Mason High School.

Families often ask about the district before anything else, so put the school names on your listing sheet or give them to a cash buyer who plans to resell.

Warren County deed transfer fees

On a Mason sale, the Warren County auditor charges a $1.00 state conveyance fee plus a $2.00 county levy for each $1,000 of price, a $3.00 combined rate. Each parcel carries a further $0.50 transfer fee, and cents in the total round up to the next dime.

Every Warren County deed travels with DTE Form 100, the statement of value, or DTE Form 100EX when the sale is exempt, and fees are made out to the county auditor. The map department initials the deed first.

Permits before closing

Mason's Engineering, Building and Planning Department handles permits through an online portal, and you can reach it at 513.229.8520. Applications cover residential building and electric work, decks, pools and spas, fences, solar, demolition, retaining walls, sewer tap-ins and signs, as well as zoning certificates.

Ask the department about any open permits or completed work without a final inspection. Unfinished permits can stall a conventional sale, and a cash buyer will usually discount for them. A zoning certificate also answers whether a property is zoned for the use a buyer has in mind.

Selling a rental in Mason

Landlords owe the Warren County Auditor a contact filing on each rental parcel, and the statute (Ohio Revised Code 5323.02) gives 60 days to update it after a change. Expect the new owner to make that filing after the deed is endorsed.

If you are selling a rented house, agree in the contract on who handles deposits, the lease and move-out dates, and keep copies of what you give the buyer.

When a cash offer suits you

A cash sale can suit sellers who want a short timeline instead of a long listing. Examples include:

  • Heirs who have inherited a house and live elsewhere.
  • Sellers of a home that needs work that would cost more than they want to spend.

Ask for any offer in writing and set it beside a realistic listing net.

What the last week looks like

Before closing, have these ready: the deed prepared with your name exactly as it appeared on the prior deed, a notary appointment, the value or exemption statement, and a mortgage payoff letter if you still owe on the house. The map department initials the deed, you pay the transfer charges at presentation, and the auditor endorses it. Taxes owed are listed on the settlement statement and paid from your proceeds, so ask the title company for a draft of that statement a few days ahead. Read each line, check the payoff figure, and raise questions before the signing appointment rather than at the table. After closing, keep your copy of the recorded deed and the settlement statement with your tax records.

Frequently asked questions

Who pays Warren County's deed fees on a Mason sale?

The seller, as grantor, pays them when the deed is presented to the auditor. Section 319.202 of the Ohio code charges both amounts to the grantor.

Does the Mason seller need to sign anything before the deed is accepted?

Yes. Under Ohio Revised Code 5301.01 the seller's signature on the deed needs a notary's acknowledgment, or that of another listed officer. Warren County also asks that the grantor's name match the previous deed.

Is a property disclosure form required in Mason?

Yes for houses of one to four units, with several exceptions. The form must be completed and handed to the buyer, and exceptions include estate transfers and relatives in the direct line.

What is the DTE 100EX form used for?

It states why a transfer is exempt from the conveyance fee. The buyer or the buyer's representative completes it, picks one of the listed reasons, and signs and dates it.

Where do I call about permits in Mason?

Call the city's Engineering, Building and Planning Department at 513.229.8520. Applications and permit fees are handled through the city's online permit portal.

Every sale moves through the same county sequence: engineer, auditor, recorder. Knowing that order ahead of time keeps the closing date from slipping. A cash buyer cannot skip those stamps either, but cash does shorten the lender-driven steps around them.

Who buys a Marion house

The average household has 2.43 people, and 84.8 percent of residents were in the same house a year earlier, so this is a settled town. Commutes average 21.0 minutes. Landlords, first-time buyers and plant workers make up much of the buyer pool, which is why a plain, working house with a sound roof and furnace sells in this market.

Marion has a long manufacturing base. Whirlpool runs a large clothes dryer factory, Nucor's mill makes rebar and signposts, and rail lines from CSX and Norfolk Southern serve an intermodal freight facility. Most of the city belongs to the Marion City School District, which runs six elementary schools, a middle school and Marion Harding High School. Buyers often ask which building serves a house. Call the district with the street address instead of assuming from the neighborhood.

U.S. Route 23 runs along the eastern edge of the city between Columbus and Findlay, and Ohio routes 4, 309 and 423 pass through. Marion sits about 50 miles north of Columbus on flat farmland, which makes for easy driving and simple lots.

Transferring a deed in Marion County

Marion County describes three stops in a fixed order. The engineer's office goes first. It compares the legal description with its records and stamps approval, and that approval is good for 60 days.

Next comes the auditor, who needs a signed conveyance form and payment before processing, then stamps the deed as transferred. The auditor's calculator page states the conveyance fee as $4.00 per $1,000 of the total sale price, plus a 50 cent line fee for each parcel. The recorder is last and checks that the deed is properly executed and carries both stamps. The recording fee is listed, effective October 17, 2019, at $34.00 for two pages and $8.00 for each additional page.

  • Engineer: legal description check and approval stamp.
  • Auditor: conveyance form, fees and transfer stamp.
  • Recorder: execution check, recording and return of the original.

The county posts the steps on its transferring property page. Phone each office to confirm today's fees ahead of closing. Because the engineer's approval lasts 60 days, line up the auditor and recorder visits right after it so the stamp does not lapse. A title company can handle all three stops for you, which is the simplest way to keep them in order.

City offices a seller should know

Marion's building department is new, and its guidance dated February 1, 2026 is organized around commercial permits and the Ohio Building Code. For a house repair, call the department at the number on its site and ask what applies to residential work.

Code enforcement sits in the police department. The officer there deals with junk motor vehicles and tires left in the public right-of-way and works with local tow companies. Posted weekday hours run Monday through Thursday, excluding holidays. An abandoned car or a pile of tires can draw a complaint, so clear the yard before you list.

The city's Contact Us page lists the police records bureau and the code enforcement phone line. Ask whether a complaint is open on your address before you sign a purchase contract.

Selling with a mortgage or liens

You can sell a house that still carries a mortgage, as long as the payoff is settled at closing. Ask your lender for a payoff letter, and have a title company search for other liens. The recorder checks that the engineer and auditor stamps are on the deed, so a lien or a missing stamp shows up at the last desk and can hold up recording.

If taxes are owed, they are paid from the sale proceeds and listed on the settlement statement. A cash buyer works the same way, and with no lender in the picture the payoff is often the only outside figure you wait on.

Marion landmarks that help a listing

The Palace Theatre, opened August 30, 1928 and restored in 1975, seats 1,440 and is one of only 16 remaining atmospheric theatres designed by John Eberson that still operate. A U.S. president lived in Marion and is buried here. The Marion Public Library serves as the main public library. These are easy details to mention when describing the setting beyond the house itself.

What to gather before you call a buyer

A simple folder of papers can save days of back and forth. Collect the deed or the name on title, the most recent property tax bill, any mortgage payoff letter, and notes on repairs you know about. Walk the yard and haul off junk vehicles and old tires. Decide what stays in the house. With those in hand you can answer a cash buyer's first questions on the spot, and the county stamps follow in order without surprises. If you are still deciding between a listing and a cash sale, ask each buyer what date they can close and what they expect you to repair.

What is the Marion County conveyance fee?

Use the transfer fee calculator on the Marion County Auditor's website, which applies the county's current rate and line fee to your sale price. Under Ohio law the seller, as grantor, pays it.

How long does the engineer's transfer stamp last?

Sixty days. After the engineer stamps the deed for transfer, finish the auditor and recorder steps inside that window or start the engineer step again.

Which school district is my Marion house in?

Most addresses fall in the Marion City School District. Others sit in the Elgin, Pleasant, Ridgedale or River Valley local districts, so verify the exact district with the schools before you advertise it.

Who handles junk cars or tires on a Marion property?

Marion's police department employs a code enforcement officer for those complaints. The phone number and weekday hours are on the city's Contact Us page.

Can I sell a Marion house with mortgage or lien problems?

Yes, provided the payoff is settled at closing. Ask your lender for a payoff letter and have a title company search for other liens, because the recorder checks that the engineer and auditor stamps are on the deed.

Choosing a fast-sale route in Brunswick

A conventional listing tends to net more on a well kept house, but it takes longer. Whichever path you choose, get the price, the closing date, and who pays each cost in writing.

Brunswick has a large base of owner-occupied single-family homes, so a clean, updated house usually finds retail buyers. A house with a wet basement, an aging roof, or open maintenance items may go faster to an investor.

Owners live in 74.7% of Brunswick homes, and 93.5% of residents stayed put for the previous year. Few neighborhoods turn over fast, which keeps competition modest. Medina County's largest city lies roughly 20 miles southwest of Cleveland, and residents report a 27.6 minute average commute. Median household income is above $90,000.

Growth since incorporation

Brunswick was founded on January 1, 1815, and became a village on February 1, 1960, then a city on October 2 of the same year. Population then took off: 11,725 in 1960, 27,645 in 1980, and 35,426 in the 2020 census. A good deal of the local housing was built in the years after incorporation.

Buyers of houses from that era ask first about the roof, furnace, water heater, and electrical panel, so gather dates and receipts for each before you list. A buyer's inspector will ask the same questions, and written answers shorten the negotiation that follows.

Building and property maintenance staff

The city's Building Division works from 4095 Center Road and answers at 330-558-6830. Call ahead for an appointment, because no permit is issued the same day it is requested.

Property maintenance and zoning enforcement sit with the same staff, who aim to abate any nuisance that drags down a neighborhood. Inspectors completed over 1,300 property maintenance inspections in a recent year. Staff also register building contractors, issue permits, schedule inspections, and check storm water runoff and sediment control to meet Ohio EPA requirements. Permit applications and contractor registrations can be left in a drop box in the City Hall vestibule that stays open around the clock.

  • For a deck, a finished basement, or an addition you built, make sure the permit was signed off.

Taxes and deeds in Medina County

Brunswick lies in Medina County. Valuation belongs to the county auditor, deed filing to the recorder, and tax collection to the treasurer. Under Revised Code 319.202 the seller bears the transfer fee.

The state homestead application used in Medina County is due December 31 for real property, and a property held by a company, partnership, or LLC does not qualify. A senior applicant must reach 65 no later than that December 31. The income cap moves over time, so get the current limit from the auditor's office.

Ohio's condition disclosure form

Revised Code 5302.30 sets out a form on which you describe your water source, sewage system, roof, foundation, and any hazards you know about, such as lead paint or radon. The signed form goes to the buyer, and a buyer who first sees it after signing the contract gets three business days to back out. Several transfers are exempt, including those by an estate fiduciary and by an heir who did not occupy the house.

Fill it out honestly and keep a signed copy. Repairs you finished, with receipts, help more than a blank line.

Who shops for Brunswick houses

The 2020 census recorded 14,714 housing units in Brunswick, with 3.6% vacant, and 14,187 households. The median age was 41.5, with 21.4% of residents below 18 and 18.0% at 65 or above. About 29.5% of households included children under 18.

The typical buyer is a family or a couple already living in the Medina and Cleveland area. Households average 2.42 people. From offer to closing

Start by deciding what matters most, a high price or a firm date. Then collect written offers and compare what each one leaves in your pocket after closing costs. Ask every buyer how they plan to pay, whether they want an inspection, and whether they expect repairs or credits.

Once you accept, a title company or closing agent orders the title search, confirms the owner of record, and prepares the deed. Bring photo identification, the keys and garage openers, and any warranties or receipts for work on the roof, furnace, or water heater. You sign the deed before a notary, the buyer's funds arrive, and the title company pays off your mortgage and any taxes owed from the proceeds.

  • Before you sign, ask the Building Division about open permits or a maintenance complaint on the address.
  • Ask the treasurer for a payoff number so the tax proration on the settlement sheet matches reality.
  • If you are behind on payments, tell the title company early so the lender's payoff letter is ready.

A cash sale skips the lender appraisal and usually the buyer's repair list, which is why it can close in a short window. Whatever you pick, read the contract for who covers the transfer fee, the prorated taxes, and any repair promises before you sign.

Where do I turn in a permit application in Brunswick?

Use the drop box in the City Hall vestibule at 4095 Center Road, which stays open around the clock. Calling 330-558-6830 first to book an appointment is the easiest route, since permits are never issued the same day.

Who enforces property maintenance rules on a Brunswick house?

The city's Building Division, through its property maintenance and zoning inspectors. Ask them whether a complaint is open on your address, because an unresolved item can surface during a sale.

Which county office records my Brunswick deed?

The Medina County Recorder files it after the Auditor handles the transfer. Your title company normally submits both, so you mainly need your parcel number and the signed deed.

Does Ohio require a condition report from a Brunswick seller?

Usually yes, using the state form described in Revised Code 5302.30. The statute lists exceptions, so ask your closing agent whether your transfer qualifies.

Does the seller or the buyer pay the transfer fee in Brunswick?

The seller. Revised Code 319.202 names the grantor, and the closing statement shows the figure.

What are my choices if a Lima house has to sell soon?

A Lima owner has three realistic paths: a listing through an agent, a private sale to a buyer already in hand, or an as-is purchase by an investor paying cash. Which one fits depends on the age of the furnace and roof, the date you need the money, and whether a tenant is still in the unit.

A listing tends to reach the widest pool of buyers and can bring the best price on a tidy house, though lender appraisals and repair requests can slow it down. A cash buyer removes the lender from the picture and lets you leave the clutter, the dated kitchen and the deferred maintenance behind. Every path still runs through the same Allen County deed steps explained further down.

  • A listing suits a cared-for house and an owner who can wait out a financed closing.
  • A private sale suits a seller who has found the buyer and needs help only with the deed.
  • A cash purchase suits an inherited, vacant or tenant-occupied house that needs repair.

Lima housing numbers

Lima is a low-priced market where renters outnumber owners. Only 45.6 percent of occupied homes are owner-occupied, so a seller will often find that the likely buyer is a local landlord rather than a family.

Location and what buyers look for

Allen County's government sits in Lima, a northwest Ohio city of roughly 13.6 square miles of land with the Ottawa River crossing it. Ohio routes 309, 65, 81 and 117 cross in Lima, Interstate 75 runs along its eastern side, and U.S. Route 30 lies a few miles to the north.

What does Ohio require a Lima seller to sign and file?

Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 obliges owners of one-to-four unit homes to hand each prospective buyer a completed disclosure form. A buyer who receives it only after contracting has three business days to cancel in writing.

Court-ordered transfers, foreclosure sales and estate transfers by a fiduciary sit outside the rule, as does a sale by someone who inherited the house and has not lived there in the last year. If your Lima house came through probate, have the closing office confirm which side of that line you are on.

The conveyance fee belongs to the seller. Section 319.202 puts the grantor on the hook, and section 319.54 prints the base fee as one dollar or ten cents per hundred dollars, whichever is greater. Counties may add their own tax under section 322.02 at up to thirty cents per hundred dollars, so ask the Allen County Auditor which rate applies to your deed.

Rental registration for Lima landlords

A Lima ordinance passed on January 2, 2024 requires each owner of a rental housing unit to hold a Rental Housing Unit Registration Certificate, and that duty applies even when the unit sits empty. Registration and updates carry no fee, and owners file through online forms after opening a CivicPlus account, as described in the city's registration notice.

Sales trigger a follow-up. A buyer who takes over a registered unit has 30 days after closing to update the record, so a landlord selling to an investor should pass along the certificate details.

  • Single-property and multi-property online forms both exist.
  • An unrented unit still needs a certificate.
  • Separate from the city rule, owners also report contact details to the county auditor.

What happens at the Allen County Auditor and Recorder?

Your deed visits two county offices in order. The auditor stamps it for transfer, and then the recorder places it in the permanent land records. The recorder takes mailed conveyances only when the auditor's conveyance stamp is already affixed.

The recorder's duties include deeds, mortgages, plats, powers of attorney and tax delinquency liens, each indexed so a title searcher can trace ownership. A document showing a Social Security number is turned away unless an affidavit comes with it. Recording fees follow the Revised Code and are printed in a schedule the office publishes, so request the current sheet before closing.

Drafting the deed and clearing old mortgages belongs to a title company or attorney. County staff explain their own steps but cannot write your documents.

Winter and the condition of the house

Cold winters put heating systems, roofs and basements under the microscope. Buyers' inspectors often flag shingles, gutters, foundation walls and furnaces first. Documenting recent work on those items, or pricing the house to reflect their age, prevents surprises. A vacant house that sits through a freeze needs steady heat or drained pipes. If you have already moved out, ask a neighbor or friend to check the house regularly, and keep any receipts for new roofing or a furnace tune-up to hand the buyer with the disclosure form.

From first call to closing in Lima

The order below keeps things moving.

  1. Decide on a listing, a private sale or a cash purchase.
  2. If the house is a rental, confirm the city certificate is current and note the buyer's 30 day update window.
  3. Deliver the disclosure form unless your transfer is exempt.
  4. Ask a title company or attorney to draft the deed and clear old mortgages.
  5. Take the deed to the Allen County Auditor for the conveyance stamp, then to the Recorder.

Can I sell my Lima house without making repairs?

Yes. Ohio sets no repair requirement for a sale, though the disclosure form must still be delivered unless your transfer is exempt. Investors who buy for cash typically price the repairs into their offer.

Who covers the transfer charges on a Lima sale?

The seller pays them. The grantor owes the state conveyance fee and any county transfer tax under section 319.202(D). Your contract may allocate other closing costs differently.

What if I rent the house I want to sell?

Confirm the city certificate is current before you list. Lima requires a rental registration for each unit, and the incoming owner must update it within 30 days of closing. County auditor contact filings are a separate duty.

Where do Lima deeds get recorded?

With the Allen County Recorder, after the Allen County Auditor stamps the document. Both are county offices located in the city, and neither is part of city hall.

What slows down a Lima closing the most?

Title problems and lender steps cause most delays. Open liens, an unsettled estate or a missing signature can hold up the auditor stamp and recording, while a cash buyer removes the appraisal and underwriting stages.

How long a Stow sale can take

Time in a sale is mostly spent waiting on other people. A listing waits for showings, a lender and an inspector, and one repair request can reopen the price. Selling on your own is only as quick as your contract and deed are. Cash has the shortest list of steps: one walkthrough, then title work and the Property Transfer Department. On the county side, a clean package filed early may be approved by evening, while a missing form or the wrong fee eats at least a day. Have the closing agent proofread every page before it goes downtown.

Paperwork to line up before closing

Collect these before a closing date is set: permit records for every deck, furnace, roof or basement project; a signed and dated disclosure form; the lease, deposit ledger and any move-out date if tenants live there; probate papers if the house came through an estate; and an answer from Summit County Sanitary Services if a sewer lateral is in doubt. Then confirm the three county charges on the settlement statement and settle in writing who pays each one.

When a cash offer is worth considering

Cash makes sense for an inherited house with put-off repairs, a tenant-occupied rental, or an owner who moved away and keeps paying two sets of bills. With a roof or sewer line nearly worn out, selling as is takes the repair decision off your plate.

Judge an offer against what a listing would net after commission and repairs. Pin down who pays the transfer charge, how long title work will take and what happens if the buyer backs out. Every answer belongs in the contract.

Who pays the county transfer charge on a Stow sale?

You do, as the seller. The county transfer tax falls on the grantor under Ohio Revised Code 322.02, and the auditor side of the Summit County Fiscal Office collects it when the deed arrives.

What inspections does the City of Stow perform?

The city inspects permitted construction work and offers same-day visits when you call before 9 am. Nothing here is a mandatory inspection at sale. Ring the Building Department on 330-689-2729 about your address, and assume the buyer will hire a private inspector.

Which office records a Stow deed?

Stow is in Summit County, so the county Fiscal Office records the deed once the transfer is approved. When you set the closing date, ask what the per-page recording charge will be.

Can I sell a Stow house that has a tenant?

Yes. Give the buyer the lease and the deposit ledger, or put a move-out date in the contract. Your landlord duties last until title changes hands.

What if I inherited a house in Stow?

For permits and property maintenance, ask City Hall directly. For deeds and value complaints, use the Cuyahoga County Fiscal Office and Board of Revision. The sections below explain what each office does.

Housing costs and who lives here

Given those ages, expect many Westlake sales to involve downsizing owners or heirs settling an estate. Of 15,508 housing units in 2020, 5.7% were vacant. Owner-occupied houses rarely sat empty (0.8%), while rentals did more often (8.5%).

Growth and shopping

Dover Village took the name Westlake in 1940 and became a city in 1957. Population jumped from 12,906 in 1960 to 27,018 in 1990 and 34,228 in 2020, which means a lot of the housing dates to the postwar decades.

Crocker Park, a mixed-use center built around a small-town street plan, holds 1,050,000 square feet of retail, 650 residential units and 100,000 square feet of office space. Workers here commute 24.4 minutes on average, a fact to mention to downtown commuters.

Valuation complaints go to the county's Board of Revision under Chapter 5715 of the Revised Code. For tax year 2026 you can file from January 1 through March 31, 2027. The statute sets the deadline at the end of March following the tax year, unless first-half collection closes later.

You'll find the board upstairs at 2079 East Ninth Street (second floor). Phone 216-443-7195 or email BORInfo@cuyahogacounty.gov. Its site posts the state forms, a searchable list of closed and pending complaints since 2018 and guidance on evidence. Ohio Revised Code 5715.19 requires a complainant to give the board all information or evidence they hold that affects the property.

Read the evidence guidance on the board's site before you file. A complainant who withholds evidence can be barred from using it on appeal.

Timeline for an as-is sale

Work backward from the day you want to close. Clear permit and complaint questions with City Hall first, so the title company finds nothing unexpected. Book your deed preparer next. Last, weigh offers by what you'd net, and get cost splits in writing.

A value dispute can only be filed between January 1 and March 31, so a fall sale shouldn't wait on one. The Board of Revision decides value, and your closing doesn't depend on its ruling.

When an offer arrives, read it for three things: the closing date, the costs assigned to you, and any repair the buyer wants fixed. A cash buyer who accepts the house as-is should say so in writing. If heirs are involved, make sure everyone who must sign the deed is lined up before you accept a closing date.

Questions to ask City Hall before listing

Skip the guesswork and put these questions to City Hall.

  • Does any permit remain open or lack a final inspection?
  • For a rental: is a license or registration required, and does it pass to the buyer?
  • Any open maintenance or zoning complaints?
  • Which sewer and water accounts need a final reading on closing day?
  • Is the signed state disclosure form ready? Under section 5302.30 sellers of one-to-four unit homes must deliver it, except in estate sales and some family transfers.

Write down each answer with the date and department. Your title company will probably ask the same things.

Once you have answers, work through the county side. Have a title company or attorney draft the deed, choose the DTE form, and check Fiscal Office requirements ahead of closing. A cash buyer can skip the lender's appraisal, but not these local and county steps. A title company or attorney does. Fiscal Office staff can't draft deeds because the county treats that as legal work. Each transfer goes with a DTE 100 or DTE 100-EX.

City Hall at 440-871-3300, open 8 am to 4 pm. Ask about any open permit that never got a final inspection and any open maintenance or zoning complaint.

Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 makes sellers of one-to-four unit homes deliver the state form to the buyer. Estates and some family transfers are exempt.

Ways to sell fast in Massillon

A Massillon owner can use a broker, sell without one, or take a straight cash purchase. Once a contract is signed, every route runs through the Stark County Auditor and the county recorder, and through Massillon's code enforcement if the property has open violations.

Condition decides a lot. A house with deferred work can lose weeks to inspection requests on a conventional sale, while a buyer paying cash typically prices the work in and skips the repair negotiation.

Streets, neighborhoods and townships

Massillon grew along the Tuscarawas River and the Ohio and Erie Canal. It sits about 8 miles west of Canton, 20 miles south of Akron and 50 miles south of Cleveland. Main Street became Lincoln Way when the Lincoln Highway came through, and a limited-access U.S. 30 bypass opened in 1971, moving through traffic to the city's southern edge.

The city spreads over the western half of Perry Township and reaches into Jackson, Tuscarawas and Bethlehem townships, with the village of Navarre on its southern border. The township and school district behind a parcel set its levies, so read the parcel record before choosing a price.

Massillon Washington High School is home to the Tigers football program, and Paul Brown Tiger Stadium seats 16,884. The Massillon Museum occupies the historic Gensemer Brothers Dry Goods building downtown, and the Lions Lincoln Theatre still screens films and hosts live theatre.

The city's parks department runs a recreation center, a senior center and 35 parks and open spaces, and the Ohio and Erie Canal Towpath Trail and the Sippo Valley Bike and Hike Trail both pass through. Shearer's Foods, Sugardale, Fresh Mark and Aqua Ohio are among local employers. Commutes average 21.5 minutes, which suits buyers who work nearby.

Rental, vacant and foreclosed properties

Massillon's Code Enforcement Department runs the city's registration program for non-owner-occupied (rental), vacant and foreclosed properties. It also enforces rules on rubbish, junk vehicles, vegetation, dangerous buildings and building permit problems, and it keeps an online case search where you can look up a violation.

Before you sell, look up your address there. An open case can slow a sale, and a decision by the department can be appealed to the Board of Building Appeals.

Rentals carry one more step under Ohio Revised Code 5323.02, a contact filing with the county auditor. Stark County sets the filing deadline at 60 days after a conveyance form reaches the auditor, with a penalty of up to $150 against the parcel if it is missed.

What the Stark County Auditor checks on a deed

Every parcel presented for transfer in Stark County first has its legal description checked by the auditor's Tax Map Department against the county's Standards Governing Conveyances. The deed itself must also meet the department's Deed Requirement Guidelines.

The same department reviews splits, combinations, easement plats, annexations and condominium declarations, and it approves legal descriptions for sheriff sales. Call it at 330-451-7341. Staff cannot give legal advice or recommend surveyors, title offices or attorneys.

Ask the Stark County Auditor for the current conveyance fee before closing, because the amount depends on the county levy. The seller bears the fee and signs the deed before a notary.

Value on the conveyance statement

For a sale, value under Ohio Revised Code 319.202 is the full consideration, counting any mortgage or vendor's lien on the property. A gift, whole or partial, is valued at the open-market price a willing buyer would pay a willing seller.

The statute bars anyone from willfully falsifying the value of the property conveyed. The statement must also address two questions: a tax reduction under section 323.152, and any use of the farm-use valuation program in the previous or current year.

If the answer to either question is yes, the grantor and grantee must sign a sworn instrument setting out the estimated amounts, so check early whether any reduction applies to you.

When a cash sale makes sense

A cash sale fits an owner who cannot fund the repairs a house needs, or a family closing out an estate. It also fits sellers who have received a code notice and would rather hand over the house than manage repairs.

  • Vacant houses face a registration requirement and the added chance of a complaint.
  • A cash buyer can often close on the date the seller needs for a move.

Whichever way you go, ask for the offer on paper and measure it against a listing's net.

Steps from offer to closing

After you accept an offer, gather the deed and look up your address in the code enforcement case search. Resolve or disclose any open case. Have a title company or attorney prepare the deed so the Tax Map Department can check the legal description. Sign before a notary, then the deed goes to the auditor and on to the recorder.

Anything you owe, whether a mortgage balance or unpaid taxes, comes out of your proceeds at closing. Ask for a draft settlement statement a few days ahead. If the house is a rental, tell the buyer about the 60-day contact filing so it is not missed. With a cash buyer there is no lender clock, so you can set a date that fits your move, and you skip the appraisal and the repair request that follow an inspection.

What is the penalty for not registering a rental with the county?

Stark County says a penalty of up to $150 may be assessed against the property. The filing is due within 60 days after a conveyance form is filed with the auditor.

Can I get more time to pay taxes on a storm-damaged Massillon house?

Possibly. After fire, flood or tornado damage worth at least a quarter of the assessed value and $2,000 of taxable value, the county board of revision can allow up to a year of extra time (Ohio Revised Code 323.17).

Do I have to give a buyer the Ohio disclosure form?

Yes for houses of one to four units, unless the sale is excluded. Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 excludes court-ordered sales, fiduciary transfers for an estate, and heirs who have not lived in the house for a year.

Who can I call at the Stark County Auditor about deed legal descriptions?

Selling a house in North Olmsted

North Olmsted sits west of Cleveland in Cuyahoga County, ZIP code 44070. Population is 31,542, down 2.8% from the 32,437 counted in April 2020. Deeds go through the county Fiscal Office downtown, and the city runs a property maintenance program that can reach a house before or after it changes hands. Both are covered below.

A house built in the postwar boom

The census counted 6,604 residents in 1950, 16,290 in 1960 and 34,861 in 1970. Much of the housing went up in that run, which makes many houses decades old. An inspector will probably focus on the roof, furnace, wiring and basement drainage. If one of those is worn out, price the house with that in mind or choose a buyer who takes it as is.

Property maintenance program

The city says the program exists to hold housing standards steady in every neighborhood. These pieces matter most to an owner planning a sale:

  • All rental one, two and three family dwellings must be registered and are inspected inside and out every year.
  • Each year the Building Division inspects the exteriors of all residential properties in one ward. Ward 4 was slated to begin in spring 2026.
  • Apartment buildings have been registered for more than 30 years and are inspected annually.
  • Complaints are inspected as they are received.

Chapter 1363 covers exterior maintenance and Chapter 1364 covers interiors. Owners with exterior issues are notified by mail and given reasonable time to fix them. Urgent items, like high grass, get a notice on the front doorknob, and the inspector named on the notice can grant extensions.

Complaints also cover structures built without permits, vehicles parked on the grass, recreational vehicles in front yards, falling gutters and broken windows. Before you list, phone the Building Division and ask whether your address carries an open notice. Clearing one is much easier before a buyer's agent finds it.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your North Olmsted house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Repair loans and help for older houses

Two outside programs are listed on the city's property maintenance page. The Cuyahoga County Home Repair Loan Program serves lower-income owners in participating communities, with eligibility based on HUD guidelines. The Heritage Home Program is open to owners of homes more than 50 years old. It offers free advice on repairs, energy efficiency and contractor bids, plus fixed-rate loans as low as 2.0% for up to 10 years on one to three unit properties.

Either one can help pay for a new roof, furnace or windows before a listing, for an owner who would rather fix than discount. Terms change, so ask each program for current eligibility and rates before you plan around them. Pick the program first and the contractor second, because the Heritage Home Program offers free advice on contractor bids.

How a deed is recorded in Cuyahoga County

One Fiscal Office now does the jobs of the old Auditor, Recorder and Engineer. A transfer cannot go through Real Estate Services without either DTE 100, a statement of value and receipt, or DTE 100-EX, which gives the reason a conveyance fee does not apply.

  • Counter service is at 2079 E. Ninth Street, 4th floor, in Cleveland, from 8:30 to 4:30 on weekdays, with recording taken until 4:00.
  • A recording fee change took effect October 24, 2024 under Ohio Senate Bill 94: $39 covers the first two pages and each further page adds $8.
  • Staff cannot give legal advice. Drafting a deed counts as practicing law under the Ohio Supreme Court, although an owner may represent themselves.
  • Ask the Fiscal Office for the conveyance fee schedule that applies on your closing date.

A title company or closing attorney normally drafts and files all of this for you.

Checklist before you list

Make these calls and checks before the sign goes up.

  1. Ask the Building Division about open notices on the address and whether your ward is next for the yearly exterior sweep.
  2. Once rented? Verify the city registration and the Fiscal Officer filing are both up to date.
  3. Tour the house as a buyer's inspector would, starting at the roof and ending in the basement, and sort problems into fix now or disclose.
  4. Have the deed and the right DTE form drafted early, along with the conveyance fee schedule for your closing date.
  5. Settle who pays which fees in writing before you sign with any buyer.

Each item you clear early is one less reason for a late price cut.

Registering a former rental with the county

If the house was a rental, R.C. 5323.02 asks the owner to register contact details with the county Fiscal Officer. The filing carries no fee, updates are due within 60 days of a change, and a $50 penalty may be added to a tax bill when the information is missing. Owners who live out of state must name an agent in Ohio.

This sits alongside North Olmsted's own rental registration, and it applies even to owners the city already has on file. Confirm both are current so the record is clean for the next owner. If you live out of state, name your Ohio agent on the filing now rather than at closing.

When a cash offer makes sense

A direct sale fits an owner with a house that needs work, little patience for showings, or an estate on a deadline. Exterior violations in a ward due for review may be easier to hand off than to repair.

Get the offer in a signed contract and set it beside a listing's net after repairs and fees. Learn who pays recording and conveyance charges. Cash skips showings, appraisal delays and most repair haggling, yet title and the deed still have to be right.

Ask any buyer for a closing date in writing, and ask what happens if the Fiscal Office returns the paperwork. A rejected deed form costs days, so whoever prepares the forms should check them against the county's page for transfers and recording before the closing appointment. If you are also dealing with a city notice, tell the buyer about it at the start so the contract can say who will clear it.

Frequently asked questions

Which office records a North Olmsted deed?

The Cuyahoga County Fiscal Office handles it through Transfer and Recording on East Ninth Street in Cleveland. Each transfer needs a DTE 100 or DTE 100-EX form.

What is the recording fee in Cuyahoga County?

Since October 24, 2024 it is $39 for the first two pages and $8 for each added page. Confirm the amount for your own document before closing.

What is a typical home value in North Olmsted?

Three ways to sell quickly in Bowling Green

Bowling Green owners generally pick among three paths: a full listing, a for-sale-by-owner deal, or an as-is sale to someone paying cash. Speed and net proceeds pull in opposite directions, so weigh both before you call anyone.

  • Full listing: the widest exposure and often the best price. You live with open houses, a buyer's inspection list, and a lender's appraisal.
  • For sale by owner: no agent fee, but you set the price, write the ad, and manage the paperwork.
  • As-is cash sale: the buyer accepts the house with its flaws, and the closing date can bend to your schedule. The offer will sit below what a repaired house earns, since the buyer prices in the work.

Houses that need a new roof, carry a tenant, or came from an estate often suit the third path. A tidy home close to the university is more likely to do well with a listing.

Bowling Green housing market

Bowling Green is a university town, and renters outnumber owners. The 2025 estimate is 31,182 residents, and about one occupied home in three is owner-occupied. Bowling Green State University occupies the northeast side of the city. In the 2020 census the median age was 24.0 and 60.4% of occupied homes were rented.

Sellers therefore meet two kinds of buyers: investors who buy near campus, and households who want the city's schools and a short drive to Toledo.

The rent, value, and income rows are survey averages for 2020 to 2024, and any single house can land far from them.

Older homes and drainage

The city stands on ground that was once the Great Black Swamp, which farmers drained in the 1800s. Its oldest big houses line Wooster Street, built during the oil boom of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

Winters bring roughly 21 inches of snow in a typical year, so inspectors who visit a house here tend to focus on the roof, the sump pump, the basement, and the heating system.

  • Houses near downtown and Wooster Street may still have their original wiring, plumbing, and windows.
  • Because the neighborhood sits on drained swamp, ask a local inspector for a written note on drainage that you can hand to buyers.
  • Student rentals near campus come with registration and inspection duties, covered next.
