Ohio paperwork for an Avon seller

Before closing, an Avon seller of a residence with one to four units fills out Ohio's disclosure form and gives it to the buyer (ORC 5302.30). Estate fiduciary sales and transfers to relatives are among the exceptions. A buyer who receives the form only after signing the contract can cancel in writing within three business days.

The deed must carry your signature, acknowledged by a notary or another official named in ORC 5301.01. A recorded deed protects the buyer, because ORC 5301.25 treats an unrecorded one as fraudulent against a later purchaser who had no notice of it. The Lorain County Auditor looks at the deed before the recorder does. Its counter takes conveyances in person or by e-file only, insists on typed forms and sends back anything incomplete, and staff cannot fill the forms out for you. Hand the job to the title company.

A cash sale or a listing in Avon?

Some sellers care more about a firm closing date than the highest price. A cash sale fits them. Listing in a high-value suburb can bring strong offers, along with staging, showings and repair requests after the buyer's inspection.

Run the numbers both ways. For a listing, subtract agent fees and repair costs, then add the mortgage, tax and utility bills that pile up while you wait. Compare the result with a direct offer. Insist on a written offer that names the closing date, and keep your signed disclosure form with the contract.

Why paperwork order matters

Sales in Avon run smoothest when the paper moves in one direction. The permit check comes first, because an open permit can stall an appraisal or scare a buyer's inspector. The disclosure form comes next, handed over with the first serious offer. After the contract, the title company works out the tax proration and any mortgage payoff, and your signed deed moves to the county auditor and then the recorder.

If a step is missing, the Lorain County Auditor returns the deed, and the closing date can slide. That is why many Avon sellers let the title office carry everything instead of filing it themselves.

Weighing repairs against selling as is

Move-in ready houses draw the strongest offers in a suburb like this, so a seller with time may do well to patch the obvious items. A roof, siding or a deck without a closed permit can drag down a financed sale. A seller short on time, money or patience can sell the house as it stands and take a lower number with fewer moving parts. Put both paths on paper and compare what you would keep in each.

Getting the house ready to close

Start with the permit check at City Hall, since an open permit is the most common surprise. Next, complete the disclosure form so you can hand it over with the first offer. Ask the treasurer for your tax balance and the title company for a payoff on any mortgage. Schedule the notary for the deed, and arrange to shut off or transfer water and sewer service on the closing date. If you are done with cold calls from buyers, register the address on the Do Not Knock list before you list.

Whether the buyer pays cash or uses a loan, the deed follows the same route through the county auditor and the recorder.

Plan the last week too. Confirm the closing time with the title company, bring a photo ID for the notary, and leave the keys, garage openers and any warranty papers for the buyer. Take final meter readings so water and sewer billing stops on your side at the right date.

Frequently asked questions

Can I rent my Avon house short term before I sell?

Check with the Zoning Department first. A 2021 city ordinance said short-term rentals are not a listed use in the residential districts and are therefore prohibited, so ask whether the rule has changed.

Who processes the deed for an Avon sale?

The Lorain County Auditor processes the transfer and the county recorder files the deed. The auditor takes conveyances in person or by e-file only, and a title company normally handles both steps.

What share of an Avon tax bill goes to the schools?

Avon Schools received 66.43% of the 2025 tax year bill. Lorain County received 19.18% and the city 10.12%.

Do I need to disclose problems when I sell in Avon?

Yes, on the Ohio disclosure form for homes with up to four units. It covers water, sewer, structure and known defects, and a buyer who gets it late can rescind within three business days.

Which permits should be closed before I sell in Avon?

Any permit for a deck, pool, shed, fence, roof, siding, finished basement or addition. Ask the Building Department at City Hall about open permits and unfinished inspections.

Just under two thirds of homes are lived in by their owners, so a sizeable share of the housing is rented. City and county permits

Reporting each move-in and move-out as it happens keeps the city file accurate, and an accurate file is one less thing for a buyer's agent to question.

Deed filing in Wood County

After closing, the deed goes to the Wood County Auditor before it reaches the recorder. Order of steps for a Perrysburg closing

Most delays come from sequence, not from any single office. Begin by pulling your permit history: ask Planning and Zoning about fences, sheds and any parked trailer, then ask Wood County Building Inspection whether any building permit is still open. Next, decide on the route, broker, solo sale or cash offer. When a cash purchase suits a Perrysburg owner

A cash buyer is worth considering when speed or condition matters more than top price: an inherited house nobody plans to fix up, a rental with tenants inside, or a job move on a short clock. The house sells with its flaws, which spares you contractors, showings and waiting on an appraisal.

Who issues a building permit for a Perrysburg house?

Wood County Building Inspection, after the City of Perrysburg has issued a zoning permit. The zoning permit must be obtained before the building permit is released.

A permit is required any time a fence changes in height, style or location. For a replacement identical in height, style and position, confirm with Planning and Zoning at 419-872-8060 before starting.

When do Wood County tax bills come due?

In February and July each year. Pay late and a 5 percent penalty applies during the first 10 days, then 10 percent.

Do Perrysburg landlords owe city income tax on rent?

Yes. The city asks owners of rental property to file a net profit income tax return for rental income and to report tenants who occupy or leave their units.

The state form under Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 applies, covering the water supply, sewer system, structure, hazardous materials and known defects, delivered to buyers promptly.

Selling a house in a university town

Ohio University sets the tone for most deals in Athens. The city is the county seat, 65 miles southeast of Columbus on the Hocking River, and the university is the top employer in Athens County. Houses range from student rentals and investor duplexes to a smaller group of owner-occupied homes on the hillsides above the river valley.

Three things decide how a quick sale goes: who is likely to buy, what the city expects of the property, and what Ohio asks of you on paper. The sections below cover each one.

How Ohio University shapes the market

The university pulls the market toward renting. Only 32.6% of Athens homes are owner-occupied. The city has 7,238 households at 2.30 people each, a median rent of $1,011 and a median home value of $247,000.

  • Many buyers of older Athens houses are landlords who plan to rent to students and staff.
  • Families tend to look near the Athens City School District buildings.
  • Faculty and staff at the Heritage College of Osteopathic Medicine add another group of local buyers.

A buyer who plans to rent the house takes on the rental rules described next.

Rental permits when you sell

Athens City Code Title 29 requires a valid permit on every residential rental. The code enforcement office reports more than 5,300 registered rental units, with health and safety inspections each year, run by four officers on a monthly schedule that the city posts online.

A tenant-occupied house brings that permit and inspection record into the sale. Call the Code Enforcement and Community Development office (28 Curran Drive, weekdays 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.) and ask whether the permit follows the house or must be reissued to the buyer.

The same office registers contractors each year and takes complaints about grass, trash, parking and zoning. Clear any open complaint on a vacant house before you list it.

Does flooding along the Hocking River affect a sale?

It can, since large parts of the city and the campus sit in the river's floodplain. The city names the Hocking River, Margaret Creek and Coates Run as its main flood sources, and its hazard plan ranks river flooding first among natural hazards, with flash flooding third. A 1969 Army Corps of Engineers project moved the channel south of town, but the risk has not gone away.

Building, filling or otherwise developing in the floodplain takes a city permit, and FEMA maps are linked from the floodplain page. Check your address there before you list, and expect a buyer's lender to do the same.

Ohio also gives owners some tax relief after a loss. Under ORC 323.17, a county board of revision may push a payment date back by up to a year when fire, flood or another event destroys at least 25% of a parcel's assessed value (and at least $2,000 of taxable value).

Offices for the common steps of an Athens sale

Two offices carry most of the load: the city's code enforcement department for property rules, and the county auditor for the deed.

The county bills the tax, and bills are typically due in March and August, with exact dates set each year by the treasurer. Ask the Athens County Treasurer for the dates on your parcel before you pick a closing day, so the title company prorates the right amount.

Two reductions may appear on your bill. Homestead covers owners aged 65 or older, owners who are permanently and totally disabled, and surviving spouses of recipients who were at least 59 at death. The Owner Occupancy Tax Reduction covers the owner's principal residence as of January 1 of the filing year.

When a cash offer makes sense

A cash offer fits when speed or condition outweighs the last few thousand dollars. A listing in Athens means showings, a buyer's inspection and a lender's appraisal, and each can delay closing or bring repair requests.

Direct buyers typically purchase as is. That helps with a rented duplex that has an open inspection item, a house with flood damage, or an inherited property nobody wants to fix. A cash sale still needs a signed deed, the disclosure form where it applies, and a tax payoff, so line those up before you accept.

Can I sell my Athens house while tenants live in it?

Yes. Ohio does not bar the sale of a rented house, and the lease usually carries over to the new owner. Since Athens requires a Title 29 permit and yearly inspections, ask the code enforcement office what a buyer must do to keep the permit in good standing.

Do I have to hand over a disclosure form in Athens?

Usually. ORC 5302.30 applies to homes with one to four units, with exceptions such as estate transfers and transfers to relatives. A buyer who receives the form late has three business days to cancel in writing.

Is my Athens house in a floodplain?

Check the FEMA maps linked on the city's floodplain page, or call the code enforcement office at 28 Curran Drive. Flood risk follows the Hocking River, Margaret Creek and Coates Run, and development in the floodplain needs a permit.

Who records the deed after an Athens sale?

The county recorder files it after the county auditor processes the transfer. ORC 5301.25 treats an unrecorded deed as fraudulent against a later buyer with no knowledge of it, so closing agents record promptly.

What if I owe the city for cutting my grass?

Pay it before closing. Athens sends a 5 day notice for grass over eight inches, hires a vendor if the owner does not cut it, and passes unpaid bills to the county auditor to be recorded as a tax lien.

How a Centerville deed reaches the county record

A slice of Centerville reaches into Greene County, so check your tax bill for the right county. For most Centerville parcels the deed goes through Montgomery County's Auditor, whose Deed Transfer Department adds a transfer or no-transfer stamp, and then to the Recorder.

A deed needs the names of buyer and seller, the legal description, the seller's signature, and a notary block. Documents are recorded the same business day they arrive, once the Auditor has stamped them. Items that need a No Transfer stamp, such as transfer on death designations and easements, are mailed or walked through the Auditor's department. Recording fees change, so get the schedule from the Recorder first.

  • Under Revised Code 319.202, the transfer fee is a seller cost.
  • Paying off a mortgage creates no new deed. The lender records a release, viewable on the county's online records search.
  • The county holds roughly 230,000 parcels, so quote your parcel number on every form.

Disputing your property value

The Montgomery County Board of Revision opens its filing period on January 1 and closes it at the end of March. Every complaint names the value you want and the reasoning behind it. Under Revised Code 5715.19 the date can run later when first-half collection closes after March 31.

The person who files must prove the case. Acceptable evidence is a sale of the property within three years, a recent appraisal, sales of similar nearby homes, a realtor's market analysis, and itemized repair estimates. Lists of other properties' assessed values, comments on neighbors' upkeep, and tax rate complaints do not count.

Hearings have been held by video or phone, 10 to 20 minutes per property. The board mails a decision within 90 days. Revised Code 5302.30 asks sellers of buildings of up to four dwellings to describe the water supply, sewage system, roof, foundation, walls, floors, and known hazards on a state form. A buyer who first receives it after signing the contract can back out within three business days.

Schools and amenities buyers ask about

The district operates two primary schools, six elementary schools, three middle schools, one high school, and an alternative high school. Elementary buildings date from 1955 through 2007, and the three middle schools are Magsig, Watts, and Tower Heights. The Washington-Centerville Public Library lists more than 380,000 items.

Miami Valley Hospital South opened in 2007 and grew into a full hospital with 60 beds by 2013, on a campus beside Interstate 675. The council-manager government has a seven-member council elected at large, and the Town Hall Theatre downtown dates to 1908.

From offer to closing

Once you accept an offer, a title company or closing agent opens the file. They search the title, confirm who owns the parcel, and prepare the deed and the settlement statement. Because part of Centerville sits in Greene County, tell them which county your parcel is in so the right auditor and recorder get the paperwork.

Bring photo identification, all keys, and the records for work on the roof, furnace, and other systems. You sign the deed before a notary, and the county auditor stamps it before the recorder files it. The title company pays off your mortgage and any taxes owed from the proceeds and sends you the balance.

  • Ask the treasurer for a payoff figure so the tax proration is right.
  • If your house is a historic stone home, gather any records of past renovations.
  • Compare offers by the amount you net after the seller-paid transfer fee and other closing costs.

A cash sale can skip the appraisal and the buyer's lender, which shortens the wait. A listing in a strong school zone may bring a higher price but needs more preparation. Whichever you choose, put the closing date and any repair promises in the written contract, and keep a signed copy of everything you hand the buyer, including the disclosure form and any receipts for completed work.

Frequently asked questions

Which county handles my Centerville sale?

Mostly Montgomery County, with a small portion of the city in Greene County. The county on your deed and tax bill has the auditor, treasurer, and recorder who process your paperwork.

Does a historic stone house in Centerville need a review before I sell?

Ask the city's planning and zoning office whether your address falls in a historic area with review rules. Settle that question before offering a buyer exterior changes.

Who bears the transfer fee on a Centerville house?

The seller. It lands on the seller under Revised Code 319.202, and the closing statement itemizes it.

When can Montgomery County owners file a value complaint?

Filing opens on New Year's Day and closes March 31. Upload your market value evidence to the county portal ten days or more ahead of the hearing.

Do I fill out the disclosure form for an inherited Centerville house?

Often not. The disclosure statute, Revised Code 5302.30, excludes estate fiduciaries and heirs who never occupied the home in the prior year. If you lived there, complete it. Your closing agent can say which case fits you.

Selling a house in Zanesville

Zanesville is the Muskingum County seat, roughly 52 miles east of Columbus, at the junction of two rivers. The population is 25,138. Renters outnumber owners here: owner occupancy is 43.8%, the median home value is $123,700, and median gross rent is $821.

With fewer than half of homes lived in by their owners, tenants are part of many sales. If your house has a tenant, tell buyers whether the lease runs past closing and who holds the deposit. Interstate 70 and U.S. 40 both run through town, which keeps commuters and travelers in the local buyer pool.

Building and code enforcement

The city's Building and Code Enforcement office, at 401 Market Street, Room 227, enforces the International Property Maintenance Code, the city's codified ordinances and the zoning code. It can start legal proceedings against violators. The doors are open weekdays from 7:30 a.m. until 4:30 p.m. Reach them at 740-617-4890.

The same office issues and inspects the permits a buyer's inspector will ask about:

  • Residential building, electrical and mechanical permits, which do not include plumbing.
  • Residential and commercial sidewalk, curb and curb cut permits.
  • Demolition permits.
  • Permits to move a house or an accessory structure wider than 14 feet or larger than 450 square feet.
  • Certificates of occupancy.

The office keeps lists of condemned properties and posts a 2026 annual vacant property form. If your house sits empty, ask whether the form applies to you before you list. For zoning questions, call Planning and Zoning at 740-617-4909. If your address is just outside the city line, South Zanesville has its own permit department at 740-454-0492.

Values, appeals and homestead in Muskingum County

For valuation and exemption questions, the Muskingum County Auditor is at the courthouse, 401 Main Street, (740) 455-7109, open weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The January 2026 tax bills reflect values set in January 2025. An addition, a demolition or newly passed levies can change a bill.

Appealing your value

Values are adjusted by the Board of Revision, which has three members: the auditor, the treasurer and the president of the commissioners, or people they designate. It cannot change how many tax dollars the county collects. Your complaint is a formal legal filing handed to the auditor between January 1 and March 31. Plan on one complaint every three years, and note that pulling one back still uses up your turn. What to expect:

  • You carry the burden of proof. The board can raise your value, cut it or leave it unchanged.
  • The hearing notice arrives by certified mail at least ten days ahead.
  • After a filing, an appraiser from the auditor may visit and propose a settlement figure. Accepting it in writing cancels the hearing.
  • A corporation should have an attorney file for it.

Homestead exemption

The Homestead Exemption is for seniors, disabled owners and surviving spouses. For tax year 2025 it takes $29,000 off taxable market value, with an income limit of $41,000 that is adjusted each year for inflation. The filing deadline is December 31. A disabled-veteran owner gets a larger reduction, equal to the tax on up to $58,000 of market value. If you receive the exemption, ask the auditor how a sale affects it on your parcel.

What a Zanesville seller must disclose

Under Ohio Revised Code 5302.30, anyone selling a one to four unit home completes a state disclosure form. Answer honestly and deliver it quickly. Errors about things you did not actually know of do not create liability for you. If the buyer gets the form late, though, they may cancel within three business days.

Gather permit numbers and any notices from the code office before showings, so the buyer sees them alongside the form. Open permits, a condemned notice or an unfiled vacant property form are the sort of loose ends that slow a closing.

Before you list: a short checklist

Make a handful of calls before the sign goes up. The city code office can tell you which permits a deck, addition, furnace or electrical panel needed, and whether an empty house must file the vacant form. The county auditor can explain your value, your homestead status and whether the January bills picked up a recent change.

Next, pull together the paperwork a buyer will want: the deed, any lease and deposit records if a tenant lives there, receipts for major repairs, and the permit numbers noted above. Fill out the state disclosure form early and slowly, since rushed answers are where honest mistakes creep in. If the house is vacant, walk through it for anything the code office could cite, such as overgrown yards, broken steps or boarded openings, and fix what you can before photos are taken.

Planning an appeal? The window shuts on March 31. If a sale could close before then, ask the auditor what happens to a pending complaint once the parcel changes owners.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Zanesville houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

When a cash offer makes sense

Consider a cash offer for a rental with tenant trouble, an inherited house or a place whose repairs would worry a lender's appraiser. It can also end the monthly cost of a vacant house that keeps drawing taxes and utility bills. With cash there is usually no lender appraisal to pass and fewer repair demands after inspection.

The usual steps are simple. First you describe the house. Then a buyer makes an offer, often after a walk-through, and you choose the closing day. A title company prepares the paperwork and records the deed. Tenants, unpaid code citations and an incomplete permit history do not disappear in a cash sale, so settle what you can with the city first and be upfront about the rest.

If your house has open code issues, ask each buyer how they would treat them and get the answer in writing before you pick a closing date. Many buyers will take a property as it stands, but read what the contract says about repairs, access and the deposit.

Get at least two written offers, line up the closing costs and dates side by side, and request the settlement statement from the title company a day or two ahead of signing.

Frequently asked questions

Who do I call about zoning in Zanesville?

Zoning questions go to the city's Planning and Zoning office, 740-617-4909. South Zanesville and several townships have separate contacts, since zoning follows the address.

How often can I appeal my Muskingum County property value?

About once every three years. The filing window is January 1 to March 31, and a complaint you withdraw still counts as your turn.

Can the Board of Revision raise my value?

Yes, it can go up. Since you must prove your case, bring a recent comparable sale, an appraisal or repair estimates.

Does a vacant house need to be registered?

The city posts an annual vacant property form for 2026. Call 740-617-4890 to learn whether your address must file before a sale.

What permits might a buyer ask me about?

A buyer's inspector may ask about residential building, electrical and mechanical permits, demolition permits and certificates of occupancy. All are issued by the city's Building and Code Enforcement office, so bring permit numbers for any addition or major system replacement.
